chunks.content: Central Message A passive PALA in a porcine surrogate LTx model prevents RVF and may reduce lung injury and inflammation compared with conventional ECMO. Perspective The optimal intraoperative support strategy in LTx remains debated. This porcine study introduces a pumpless PALA that effectively prevents RVF. Additionally, it may reduce pulmonary injury and inflammation compared with ECMO. These findings suggest that the pumpless approach is a promising strategy with potential clinical benefits. The need for intraoperative extracorporeal life support (ECLS) during bilateral lung transplantation (LTx) remains highly debated. Historical use of cardiopulmonary bypass has shifted to venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO). , , The ongoing discussion concerning the optimal intraoperative ECLS strategy is fueled by differences in indications, clinical protocols, cannulation strategies, and circuit configurations. , Some use ECLS routinely, and others use it on indication. , Despite the efforts to compare off-pump and on-pump bilateral LTx, there remains a paucity of clinical data from well-designed prospective trials. , We lack comprehensive mechanistic and physiological understanding to better guide clinical implementation and optimalization of ECLS strategies. For instance, the relation between ECLS and primary graft dysfunction (PGD) still needs to be fully elucidated. Clinically, ECLS can support gas exchange and provide hemodynamic stabilization, such as in severe PGD, RV strain and failure, and settings where only 1 native or transplanted lung during bilateral LTx is in situ. Avoiding ECLS-related complications remains challenging. These include bleeding disorders, thromboembolic events, and vascular and wound cannulation site complications. , , Furthermore, ECLS can be responsible for an additional inflammatory hit. , , We recently reported on the complexity of right ventricular (RV) interaction with pulmonary ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) severity during bilateral LTx. In a porcine pulmonary IRI model, we demonstrated that higher pulmonary flows and pressures aggravated IRI severity. In parallel, IRI had a major impact on RV function. An important remaining question is how ECLS might impact or modify the physiological changes we observed in this model and if there is an opportunity to further refine and develop alternative ECLS configurations based on clear hemodynamic and respiratory parameters. A promising strategy might be to drain blood from a cannula in the pulmonary artery (PA) and return it through a cannula in the left atrium (LA) with a low resistance oxygenator in between. This passive pumpless strategy (PA to LA bypass [PALA]) has been successfully adopted as bridge to LTx in a limited number of patients. , , , , , , , PALA might have theoretical benefits, such as reduced blood activation (less blood surface contact and no mechanical pump), while maintaining the hemodynamic and respiratory support of conventional intraoperative ECLS. The aim of this study is to assess the hemodynamic and respiratory effects of PALA and conventional VA-ECMO in our animal model of severe IRI. Material and Methods This experimental porcine study (Strain: TN70, Topigs Norsvin) was approved by the Ethics Committee on Animal Research KU Leuven (P0115/13-01-2020). Consent was not required due to nature of study. All animals received human care in accordance with Principles of Laboratory Animal Care, formulated by the National Society for Medical Research and Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, prepared by the Institute of Laboratory Animal Resources and published by the National Institutes of Health (Publication No. 86-23, revised 1996). Experimental Protocol Twenty-seven male pigs were divided into 3 groups: group 1, clamping (CLA; n = 9) ; group 2, PA to LA oxygenator (PALA; n = 9); and group 3, centrally cannulated VA-ECMO (ECMO; n = 9). Anesthesia maintenance, surgical procedure, and sampling for the CLA group were previously described. Our porcine model is based on sequential clamping and unclamping of the left or right PA and was developed to simulate the intraoperative hemodynamic phases of bilateral LTx ( , A ). First, the left pulmonary artery (LPA) and left main bronchus were clamped for 3 hours (1-3 hours). Second, the ischemic left lung (LL) was reperfused for 2 hours (4-5 hours). Finally, the RPA was clamped for 1 hour (6 hours) to direct the whole right ventricular cardiac output (RV CO) toward the postischemic injured LL. Clamping group Sequential pulmonary clamping and unclamping were performed to create severe pulmonary IRI and RV strain, corresponding with intraoperative bilateral LTx. No ECLS was used. Pulmonary artery to left atrium bypass group In addition to the surgical procedures of CLA, an extracorporeal bypass with a low-resistance oxygenator was inserted between the main PA and LA auricle (Hemovent GmbH). Anastomosis between 3/8 tubing and the tissue was facilitated with vascular grafts (Gore-Tex Vascular Grafts, WL Gore and Associates, Inc). For the PA, a 13-mm graft was used. For the LA, an 8-mm graft was used. For the LA, a 21F arterial cannula (Maquet, Getinge) was connected to the graft to avoid kinking. A flow probe

RV strain, corresponding with intraoperative bilateral LTx. No ECLS was used. Pulmonary artery to left atrium bypass group In addition to the surgical procedures of CLA, an extracorporeal bypass with a low-resistance oxygenator was inserted between the main PA and LA auricle (Hemovent GmbH). Anastomosis between 3/8 tubing and the tissue was facilitated with vascular grafts (Gore-Tex Vascular Grafts, WL Gore and Associates, Inc). For the PA, a 13-mm graft was used. For the LA, an 8-mm graft was used. For the LA, a 21F arterial cannula (Maquet, Getinge) was connected to the graft to avoid kinking. A flow probe (Terumo Corporation) was placed on the tubing toward the oxygenator. The extracorporeal bypass was opened at the moment of LPA clamping. No mechanical pump was inserted ( , B and , A ). Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation group In addition to the surgical procedures of CLA, a central VA-ECMO was installed. An arterial 18F cannula (Medtronic) was inserted in the thoracic aorta and a 22F venous cannula (Maquet, Getinge) was inserted in the right atrium. A configuration comparable to the clinical setting was used with a centrifugal pump (Rotaflow; Maquet, Getinge), an oxygenator (CAPIOX FX15; Terumo Corporation), and a heat exchanger ( , B and , B ). Flow through the extracorporeal circuit in both the PALA and ECMO groups was initiated at the time of LL clamping, following baseline (BL) measurements. To obtain a fair comparison between the 2 ECLS strategies, ECMO flow rates were adjusted to be comparable to PALA, based on preliminary data. In all groups, RV failure (RVF) was defined as an acute decrease of RV CO greater than 50% or death of the animal before completing the protocol that could not be otherwise explained (bleeding, arrhythmia). At the end of the experiment, all animals were euthanized. Sampling and Data Collection Hemodynamic and respiratory parameters ( ) were recorded continuously using ICM+ (Cambridge Enterprise). Blood gases were taken hourly (arterial, PA, left and right lower pulmonary veins). Plasma was sampled for troponin-T and cytokine analysis (BL and 6 hours): interleukin (IL)-1b, IL-12p40, IL-4, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, interferon (IFN)-α, IFN-γ, and tumor necrosis factor-α. RV monitoring was performed using a conductance catheter (Ventri-Cath 507, Millar Instruments) to measure RV pressure-volume (PV) loops. Details of catheter positioning, recording and analysis were previously described. RV end-systolic pressure (ESP), end-diastolic pressure, stroke volume (SV), stroke work (SW), arterial elastance (Ea), end-systolic elastance (Ees), RV-PA coupling, and pressure-volume area were measured or calculated. Flow probes around main PA and LPA (Transonic Systems Inc) were placed. Pulmonary, LA, and arterial blood pressures were invasively measured. Pulmonary vascular resistance was determined by subtracting the LA pressure from the mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP), dividing the result by the CO reaching the pulmonary vasculature. The value was then multiplied by 80 to express pulmonary vascular resistance in dyn·s·cm −5 . At the end of the experiment, the heart-lung block was surgically removed, and samples were taken for pulmonary wet-to-dry weight ratio (W/D) and RV free wall histological evaluation. Subsequently, the inflated lungs were frozen in nitric oxide vapors. Ex vivo computed tomography (CT) (Siemens Healthcare) of the frozen lungs was performed to quantify parenchymal density as a marker of pulmonary injury. Analysis was performed in HOROS program (DICOM Viewer, v.3 GPL-3.0). , A parenchymal sample was taken from the center of left lower lobe. Histology evaluation (hematoxylin-eosin) of both RV and LL tissue samples was performed by an experienced and blinded pathologist. Pulmonary samples were scored on the presence of interstitial edema, intra-alveolar edema, hemorrhage, interstitial cell infiltration, intra-alveolar neutrophile infiltration, and hyaline membranes. Ventricular samples were scored on presence of inflammatory infiltrates, edema, fibrosis, myocyte damage, and endocardial lining damage. A semiquantitative scoring system was used of 0 to 3 (0 = absent; 1 = mild; 2 = moderate; 3 = severe), and a total score was reported. , , Statistical Analysis An a priori power analysis was conducted based on our previously published data. To obtain a significant difference between the CLA and intervention groups (PALA and ECMO) in W/D ratio, IL-6 and LPA flow with a significance criterion of α = 0.05 and power = 0.80, the minimum sample size needed was 7 animals in each group. The data were analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software Inc) and are presented as mean ± SD. Groups were compared with 1-way analysis of variance. To compare groups in time, repeated-measures 2-way analysis of variance and a Sidak post hoc multiple comparison were used. Results Study Groups We performed 27 animal experiments. Four experiments failed due to sickness of the animal (n = 1) and technical complications of the procedure (n = 3). All complications were related to ECLS cannulation. One animal in the ECMO group experienced an acute, unintentional aortic decannulation resulting in

7 animals in each group. The data were analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software Inc) and are presented as mean ± SD. Groups were compared with 1-way analysis of variance. To compare groups in time, repeated-measures 2-way analysis of variance and a Sidak post hoc multiple comparison were used. Results Study Groups We performed 27 animal experiments. Four experiments failed due to sickness of the animal (n = 1) and technical complications of the procedure (n = 3). All complications were related to ECLS cannulation. One animal in the ECMO group experienced an acute, unintentional aortic decannulation resulting in substantial blood loss, and 2 animals in the PALA group sustained significant hemorrhage from the LA cannulation site. After refinement of the cannulation technique, including the use of vascular grafts and improved cannula fixation. No further such events occurred. Consequently, we included n = 9 animals from the CLA group, n = 7 animals in PALA, and n = 7 animals in ECMO groups. The weight of the animals was comparable among all 3 groups ( ). Details of all comparisons ( P values) are presented in . Pulmonary Injury Assessment Pulmonary injury is quantified in and . The W/D ratio ( , A ) was significantly higher in ECMO compared with PALA. No significant difference was measured between CLA and PALA or CLA and ECMO. Histology injury score ( , B ) was comparable among all 3 groups. Oxygenation (left pulmonary vein pO 2 ; , C ) significantly decreased over time in all 3 groups. Quantification of CT-measured density ( , D and E ) was not significant between groups but tended to be lower in PALA versus ECMO. Blood Flow Through Extracorporeal Circuit and Postischemic Lung Blood flow is quantified in and . As intended by the experimental protocol, we observed that flows in PALA and ECMO ( , A ) were comparable at all time points. Also, these remained stable throughout the experiment, despite different ECLS configurations ( , B and ). We used acute decrease of RV CO greater than 50% as a marker of RVF. In CLA, 5 of 9 animals developed RVF during 6 hours after right lung clamping. No animal in PALA or ECMO developed RVF. Flow toward ECMO was deviated from the right atrium. In PALA, flow was deviated from the PA after it was ejected by the RV ( , B ). Consequently, RV CO ( , B ) in ECMO was lower than in CLA and PALA, with the exception of CLA versus ECMO at 6 hours. However, this did not affect our definition of RVF, because the decrease in RV CO was not acute. In CLA, the flow through the LPA ( , C ) increased dramatically at 6 hours compared with BL and 5 hours (after right lung clamping without supportive device). In PALA, the LPA flow increased at 6 hours compared with BL and 5 hours. In ECMO flow remained stable. However, at 6 hours, a difference was observed between CLA and ECMO. Right Ventricle Function We assessed RV function and its loading conditions based on hemodynamic parameters ( and ) and conductance catheter-derived analysis ( and ). Right ventricle hemodynamics Heart rate ( , A ) increased significantly in CLA and PALA from BL to 6 hours and remained stable in ECMO. mPAP ( , B ) increased over time in all groups. After the mechanical clamping of the LL, mPAP increased significantly in CLA, but remained stable in PALA and ECMO. Likewise, at the end of the experiment after clamping of the right lung, the mPAP increased significantly in CLA and ECMO. Calculated pulmonary vascular resistance ( , C ) revealed an increase from BL to 6 hours in all groups. At 6 hours, pulmonary vascular resistance was significantly higher in ECMO compared with CLA. Right ventricle conductance catheter-derived analysis The parameters obtained from conductance catheters enable a detailed assessment of 3 key hemodynamic variables: preload (RV SV and RV SW), afterload (Ea), and contractility (Ees). The RV SV ( , A ) was lower in ECMO compared with CLA at 1 hours, 2 hours, 3 hours, and 4 hours and in ECMO compared with PALA at 4 hours and 6 hours. A significantly lower RV SW (the mechanical work to eject SV) ( , B ) at 6 hours was observed in CLA compared with PALA. Furthermore, in CLA a decrease was noted between BL and 6 hours, reflecting RVF. Ea ( , C ) was higher in ECMO compared with CLA in 3 to 6 hours, as well as in ECMO compared with PALA at 4 hours and 6 hours. Ea increased in all groups from BL to 6 hours. Ees ( , D ) at 6 hours was lower in CLA

with PALA at 4 hours and 6 hours. A significantly lower RV SW (the mechanical work to eject SV) ( , B ) at 6 hours was observed in CLA compared with PALA. Furthermore, in CLA a decrease was noted between BL and 6 hours, reflecting RVF. Ea ( , C ) was higher in ECMO compared with CLA in 3 to 6 hours, as well as in ECMO compared with PALA at 4 hours and 6 hours. Ea increased in all groups from BL to 6 hours. Ees ( , D ) at 6 hours was lower in CLA compared with PALA, in CLA compared with ECMO, and in PALA compared with ECMO. Furthermore, it increased at 6 hours compared with BL in ECMO and PALA. A significant difference in RV coupling (energy transfer between RV and pulmonary circulation; , E ) was measured at 6 hours between CLA and PALA. The RV pressure-volume area (total RV mechanical energy; , F ) increased at 1 hour after LL clamping in both CLA and PALA compared with ECMO. Biomarkers Results of cytokine protein level analysis ( and ) showed a significant increase in IL-6 ( , A ) for each group between BL and 6 hours. At 6 hours, IL-6 was highest in ECMO compared with both CLA and PALA. No other cytokine showed a significant difference among all 3 groups. However, at 6 hours, IFN-α, IL-1β, IL-12, IL-4, and IL-10 peaked in ECMO versus CLA. Finally, tumor necrosis factor-α showed a significant decrease in all 3 groups from BL to 6 hours. Plasma analysis of troponin-T was performed. In all 3 groups, an increase was observed from BL to 6 hours ( ). Histology No significant difference was shown on RV histology in any of the measured parameters. Discussion The routine use of ECLS in LTx is intensively debated. In this study, we investigated a new strategy for intraoperative ECLS support in LTx, referred to as “PALA.” We compared it with the gold standard VA-ECMO in a porcine model of severe pulmonary IRI. Both PALA and ECMO prevented RVF. However, ECMO appears to result in increased pulmonary edema and systemic inflammation. The rationale behind intraoperative ECLS use is multiple. First, the reduction of pulmonary blood flow and mechanical shear stress through the newly transplanted graft could reduce PGD and support the respiratory function. , Second, the unloading of the RV could prevent its failure. , We previously demonstrated that predicting RVF based on physiological variables remains extremely challenging, especially in a setting of severe pulmonary IRI injury and RV strain. This is due to the complex interplay among a triad of RV preload, afterload, and contractility. , Hemodynamics and Right Ventricle When analyzing the recorded flows (extracorporeal/RV CO/LPA), we observed that the PALA circuit despite the absence of a mechanical pump maintained reliable flow across all hemodynamic phases of the experiment that prevented RVF. Ukita and colleagues investigated optimal ECLS strategies for RVF in a large animal model, including the PALA strategy (n = 2). Unlike in our study, their model failed to achieve sufficient flow due to technical limitations related to PA cannula size. RV-driven flow through the PALA circuit in our experiments remained stable, possibly due to the use of a specific low-resistance oxygenator. Both PALA and ECMO strategies successfully prevented RVF, in contrast to the CLA group without ECLS, in which half of the animals developed RVF. Notably, we found the highest afterload (expressed as Ea) in the ECMO group. We speculate that this might be due to observed increased pulmonary injury and systemic inflammation. Another cause could be higher transpulmonary pressure gradient after aortic cannulation. , Moreover, both the components of the extracorporeal circuits (specifically, the absence of a mechanical pump and heat exchanger in PALA) and the hemodynamic effects differ between the 2 extracorporeal strategies. Although ECMO primarily reduces RV preload (RV SV, RV SW), PALA reduces RV afterload (Ea), further research is necessary to elucidate the exact contribution of these differences not only to RV afterload but also to pulmonary injury and systemic inflammation. We did not detect differences in RV ischemic injury (troponin-T) between the groups. Additionally, no morphological injury was found, likely due to the duration of experimental protocol. On the basis of the hemodynamic parameters, the PALA strategy proved effective in preventing RVF in our experiments. Consequently, further investigation of its hemodynamic characteristics and potential clinical applications is warranted, because it appears to reduce afterload more efficiently than ECMO at comparable extracorporeal flow rates. Pulmonary Injury A unique aspect of our study is that we did not focus only on the hemodynamic impact of ECLS, but related our findings to the severity of pulmonary IRI. likely due to the duration of experimental protocol. On the basis of the hemodynamic parameters, the PALA strategy proved effective in preventing RVF in our experiments. Consequently, further investigation of its hemodynamic characteristics and potential clinical applications is warranted, because it appears to reduce afterload more efficiently than ECMO at comparable extracorporeal flow rates. Pulmonary Injury A unique aspect of our study is that we did not focus only on the hemodynamic impact of ECLS, but related our findings to the severity of pulmonary IRI. Severe pulmonary edema was observed in all groups. However, it was higher in ECMO compared with PALA, as expressed by the W/D ratio. The same trend was observed in CT-measured density. This is an important consideration for clinical decision-making when using ECMO and highlights PALA as a promising pulmonary protective strategy. Although pulmonary injury was assessed at multiple levels, no differences between groups were observed in histological injury scores or oxygenation levels. This may be due to the limited duration of the experimental observation period. Systemic Inflammation In parallel, we measured systemic cytokines that are known biomarkers of pulmonary IRI. We observed the highest levels of IL-6 in ECMO animals at the end of the experiment compared with both CLA and PALA. In addition, several other cytokines were significantly higher in ECMO group than CLA, whereas the results were not significant for CLA versus PALA. This may indicate an additional systemic inflammatory hit caused by the ECMO configuration, which seems to be less pronounced in PALA. This is in accordance with recent findings. Coster and colleagues reported higher endothelial injury and PGD grade 3 rates with extracorporeal support compared with off-pump. Chacon-Alberty and colleagues also reported a significantly higher systemic cytokine activation in patients who underwent LTx on ECMO versus off-pump. In their study, the measured inflammatory biomarkers increased between 0 and 6 hours post-transplant, highlighting the importance of time in the development of a full systemic inflammatory response. Although our results demonstrated differences between groups in a single cytokine, it cannot be excluded that with a longer experimental observation period, differences in additional cytokines might emerge. Possible Clinical Implications In addition to our observations, the PALA strategy offers other potential advantages over VA-ECMO. First, the absence of a mechanical pump and suction events could reduce the blood activation and trauma leading to hemolysis. The shorter and simpler circuit requires less priming volume, preserves pulsatility, and is potentially less expensive. Despite the potential physiological advantages, PALA should be considered an alternative rather than a replacement for ECMO. Potential disadvantages of PALA result from passive nature of the setup and limited control of flow through the gas exchanger. Therefore, in case of acute RVF despite PALA, a rapid switch to active support, such as VA-ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass, would be required. It is also unclear what the optimal anticoagulation strategy would be. On the one hand, lower heparinization seems acceptable due to a smaller circuit. However, in case of low flow, risk of clotting might increase. Although recent expert consensus statements are available, , we are confronted with a large gap of prospective evidence on optimal intraoperative ECLS strategies in LTx. The PALA strategy might be of interest in centers that use ECMO on indication to avoid ECMO-related complications. Patients with pulmonary fibrosis and severely reduced perfusion to 1 lung could potentially benefit from this approach. A recent study from our group demonstrated that in an off-pump LTx transplanting the right lung first leads to less PGD. However, this remains challenging for patients with severely reduced LL perfusion. In these patients, PALA could prevent escalation of RV strain to RVF. Also, the pathophysiological gradient between the PA and LA pressures in patients with secondary pulmonary hypertension would promote the passive flow through the PALA circuit. Limitations This study has several limitations. First, porcine anatomy and physiology are not identical to humans. Second, no actual (allo) transplantation has been performed. Although our model is designed to be representative of bilateral LTx hemodynamics and severe IRI leading to PGD, not all PGD-related factors are addressed. Furthermore, the RVs in our porcine model were healthy at BL, which is not the case in patients with chronic pulmonary parenchymal or vascular disease. Also, only male animals were included in this study due to logistical constraints. Future studies should aim to include both sexes. Furthermore, based on the design of our study, the effect of ECMO on the RV afterload in the context of pulmonary IRI could not be elucidated in detail. More experiments would have to be performed with different flows through the ECMO circuit. This could also provide us with more insight on pulmonary injury and cytokine activation. Last, atrial clamping, which occurs during clinical LTx, was not performed in this study. Assessing the impact of atrial clamping on

Furthermore, based on the design of our study, the effect of ECMO on the RV afterload in the context of pulmonary IRI could not be elucidated in detail. More experiments would have to be performed with different flows through the ECMO circuit. This could also provide us with more insight on pulmonary injury and cytokine activation. Last, atrial clamping, which occurs during clinical LTx, was not performed in this study. Assessing the impact of atrial clamping on flow dynamics within the passive circuit should be addressed in future studies. Conclusions In our experimental setup, both PALA and ECMO prevented RVF. Furthermore, PALA might have the potential to provide better pulmonary graft protection with less systemic inflammation activation than ECMO. Further research is necessary to compare PALA with ECMO, with a focus on the impact of individual extracorporeal circuit components on pulmonary injury and systemic inflammation. The evidence presented in this study may contribute to further development of clinical algorithms for ECLS and suggests a promising possibility for further refinement of pumpless strategies in LTx. documents.title: ISHLT consensus document for the selection of lung transplant candidates 2021 update

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a devastating disease process with complex pathogenesis and multi-factor interaction, which is characterized by progressive pulmonary vascular resistance, and ultimately leads to right ventricular failure and premature death [ , ]. PH affects approximately 1% of the global population, with the estimated incidence and prevalence higher in economically developed countries, ranging from 1.5 to 32 cases and 12.4 to 268 cases per million adults, respectively [ , ]. Over the past two decades, there has been a sea change in the understanding of the pathological mechanisms, diagnosis, and treatment algorithms of PH. Intravenous epoprostenol was a milestone in the medical treatment of patients with PH, which has been transformed into individualized multi-pathway combination medication strategies based on risk stratification [ , ]. Although the introduction of various targeted therapies has resulted in significant advances in the treatment of PH, none of the currently approved medical therapies are considered to be a definite cure, and the 5-year mortality rate remains high at about 20–60% [ ]. In real-world clinical practice, some patients fail to achieve an adequate clinical response despite receiving maximal medical treatment. At this time, lung transplantation (LTx) is the ultimate therapeutic option to save the lives of patients with severe PH [ ]. Decisions regarding the referral and listing time for LTx have been challenging in patients with PH since the disease course of PH is highly heterogeneous and unpredictable [ ]. It has been reported that patients with PH tend to have the highest mortality rate on LTx waiting lists, ranging from 18% to 41%. In addition to the inherent severity of the disease, another noteworthy reason lay in that many patients deteriorated very rapidly after prolonged medical treatment, and thus patients with severe PH were prone to miss the optimal referral and transplantation window on account of delayed referral and listing, as well as a shortage of donor organs [ , , ]. Therefore, the contradiction between adequate medical treatment and the appropriate timing of LTx referral and listing is currently a highly concerning and highly controversial topic in the PH field. In addition, concepts related to PH are changing constantly, which makes individualized treatment algorithms even more confusing. The 2021 consensus document for the selection of lung transplant candidates from the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) has introduced fresh recommendations for LTx for patients with PH based on objective risk stratification, emphasizing the significance of early referral and listing [ ]. This article will review the evolving PH-related concepts and highlight the optimization of LTx referral and listing for patients with PH, aiming to contribute to facilitating successful LTx and improving the survival outcomes of patients with severe PH. 2. Evolving Disease Concepts Associated with PH 2.1. Hemodynamic Definition and Classification of PH Since the first World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) in 1973, PH has been defined as mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) ≥ 25 mmHg at rest, measured by right heart catheterization in the supine position [ ]. With the deepening of PH clinical and translational medicine research, it has been recognized that this upper limit of normal mPAP of 25 mmHg was somewhat empirical and arbitrarily defined [ ]. Until 2018, the sixth WSPH redefined PH as mPAP > 20 mmHg at rest and added the parameter of pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) based on the pulmonary arterial wedge pressure (PAWP) to better distinguish between pre-capillary PH and post-capillary PH [ ]. Based on the 2015 ESC/ERS guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of PH (ESC/ERS PH Guidelines) and the sixth WSPH, the latest 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines adopted this new standard and introduced a transformative update of PH-related concepts [ , , ]. The new clinical classifications of PH are as follows: Group 1—pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH); Group 2—PH associated with left heart disease; Group 3—PH associated with lung diseases and/or hypoxia; Group 4—PH associated with pulmonary artery obstructions; and Group 5—PH with unclear and/or multifactorial mechanisms. Of these, PAH (Group 1), the narrative object group of this review, is the focus of current clinical practice [ , ]. 2.2. Risk Stratification of Patients with PAH Over the decades, various calculators have been designed to distinguish the severity and predict outcomes of patients with PAH [ , , , , , , ]. The US Registry to Evaluate Early and Long-term PAH Disease Management risk calculator (REVEAL risk calculator), and the ESC/ERS PH Guidelines risk table are two of the most commonly used risk stratification tools. The original REVEAL risk calculator was an algorithm that used 12 baseline parameters to calculate the risk score, predicting 12-month survival and providing useful serial survival assessments for patients with PAH [ , , ]. REVEAL 2.0 risk calculator was a modification of the original REVEAL risk

designed to distinguish the severity and predict outcomes of patients with PAH [ , , , , , , ]. The US Registry to Evaluate Early and Long-term PAH Disease Management risk calculator (REVEAL risk calculator), and the ESC/ERS PH Guidelines risk table are two of the most commonly used risk stratification tools. The original REVEAL risk calculator was an algorithm that used 12 baseline parameters to calculate the risk score, predicting 12-month survival and providing useful serial survival assessments for patients with PAH [ , , ]. REVEAL 2.0 risk calculator was a modification of the original REVEAL risk calculator, incorporating a new variable (all-cause hospitalization) and a revised variable (renal function measured by estimated glomerular filtration rate) [ ]. However, the limitations of the commonly used REVEAL risk calculator include the relatively short prediction period (1 year) and the large number of variables required (from 12 to 14 variables) at follow-up assessment. A previous study showed that simplified versions of the REVEAL scores utilizing high-yield variables appeared to have comparable performance to the original REVEAL risk calculator, which requires more in-depth data to validate [ ]. In addition, PAH patients can be classified as low-risk, intermediate-risk, or high-risk for clinical worsening or death using the 2015 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines risk table [ ]. The main evaluation parameters include clinical signs of right heart failure, syncope, World Health Organization (WHO) functional class, six-minute walk test (6 MWT), cardiopulmonary exercise testing, N -terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) plasma levels, imaging (echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI)), and hemodynamics [ ]. It was reported that, based on 12-month mortality, the correspondence between the low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups as defined by the 2015 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines and the REVEAL 2.0 risk calculator (14 variables) was as follows: low-risk = REVEAL score ≥ 6; intermediate-risk = REVEAL score 7 and 8’ and high-risk = REVEAL score ≥ 9 [ , ]. To deal with the fact that 1-year mortality was sometimes higher than predicted in patients with moderate–high risk PAH and that 60–70% of patients are classified as intermediate risk, the latest 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines presented a transformative improvement in the methods and parameters for risk stratification in patients with PAH [ , , ]. For risk stratification at initial diagnosis, a three-strata model (based on estimated 1-year mortality rates of <5%, 5–20%, and >20%, respectively) will be recommended, with as many variables included as possible for a comprehensive assessment; while at follow-up, the simplified four-strata model will be preferred, classifying patients into low-risk, intermediate–low-risk, intermediate–high-risk, and high-risk [ ]. It should be noted that the three-strata model further expanded the risk stratification factors to include echocardiography, cMRI, and some others, which would be a more accurate and scientific assessment, but these indicators were difficult to obtain in clinical practice. Collectively, the available research supported a risk-based approach that ultimately enabled patients with PAH to achieve and/or maintain a low-risk status, or to consider the timing of the referral and listing for a potential LTx [ , , ]. It is worth mentioning that the current risk stratification tools are not perfect and will be gradually optimized with the deepening of the understanding of PAH. Therefore, the combined use of multiple risk stratification tools may provide more information on survival prediction for patients with PAH [ ]. 3. Treatment Algorithms for Patients with PAH With the clinical application of vasodilatory drugs, the survival time of patients with PAH has increased from 2.8 years in the 1980s to more than 7 years in the modern era [ ]. The main clinical treatment drugs include prostacyclin, endothelin receptor antagonists (ETRAs), phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors (PDE5is), soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators (sGCs), and so forth [ , , , , , , , , , ]. However, there have been no definitely effective drugs to reverse or cure the PAH progression [ ]. The contribution of LTx to saving the lives of patients whose condition is difficult to optimize with medical treatment is the focus of this review. Organ transplantation, including heart–lung transplantation (HLTx) and LTx for PAH, is a young field, the main principle of which is that transplant programs should be positively considered when patients with PAH continue to deteriorate despite receiving optimized medical treatment [ , ]. In 1963, James Hardy and colleagues performed the first human LTx. Unfortunately, the patient survived only eight days postoperatively [ ]. There was no significant progress in LTx for the next 15 years, until the 1980s when cyclosporine was first applied as an immunosuppressive therapy, a major milestone in LTx history. In 1981, Stanford University performed the first successful HLTx on a patient with “primary pulmonary hypertension” and incorporated the concept of HLTx/LTx into clinical practice for severe PAH [ ]. Shortly thereafter,

positively considered when patients with PAH continue to deteriorate despite receiving optimized medical treatment [ , ]. In 1963, James Hardy and colleagues performed the first human LTx. Unfortunately, the patient survived only eight days postoperatively [ ]. There was no significant progress in LTx for the next 15 years, until the 1980s when cyclosporine was first applied as an immunosuppressive therapy, a major milestone in LTx history. In 1981, Stanford University performed the first successful HLTx on a patient with “primary pulmonary hypertension” and incorporated the concept of HLTx/LTx into clinical practice for severe PAH [ ]. Shortly thereafter, with the first long-term successful single LTx and significant advances in bilateral sequential LTx, the selection of LTx has become recognized as an effective treatment for PAH [ , , , ]. Formerly, HLTx and single LTx were the preferred treatments for patients with PAH. However, it is currently more popular for patients with PAH to receive bilateral LTx in most cases [ , , , , ]. Impaired ventilation–perfusion mismatching may occur after a single LTx, which may lead to subsequent rejection, infection, primary graft dysfunction (PGD), and even severe hypoxia or early death after surgery (20% mortality risk within 1 month). Additionally, potential right ventricular dysfunction and high pulmonary blood flow after a single LTx can increase the incidence and severity of PGD [ ]. In a single-center experience, the 5-year survival rate of recipients with PAH who underwent bilateral LTx and single LTx reached 84% and 51%, respectively, which further clarified the survival benefit of bilateral LTx [ ]. Moreover, a severe shortage of heart–lung blocks has been a significant obstacle in the field of HLTx, and henceforth HLTx will be reserved for patients with other uncorrectable heart conditions, including Eisenmenger syndrome complicating complex congenital heart disease (CHD), failed CHD repair, uncorrectable CHD, and severe left ventricular failure [ ]. Another reason for this transformation is the growing understanding that the primary pathophysiological variation of PAH is in the pulmonary vessels, rather than inherent right ventricular problems [ ]. Actually, studies have shown that pressure-overloaded right ventricles can be remodeled and recovered after bilateral LTx [ , , ]. Previously, we reviewed 10 studies in end-stage cardiopulmonary disease, which involved 1230 patients with bilateral LTx and 1022 patients with HLTx. The results showed that 1-year, 3-year, 5-year, and 10-year survival rates were comparable between the two groups [ ]. Also, bilateral LTx has the advantages of shorter waiting times and greater donor allocation. Since the 2010s, consensus statements for the selection of lung transplant candidates have supported bilateral LTx as the primary surgical treatment for severe PAH [ ] ( , ). 4. LTx Referral Time for Patients with PAH 4.1. Dilemmas of Transplant Referral In the golden age of LTx, the selection of LTx for patients with PAH remained much rarer than for other diseases [ ]. In the early stages, LTx for patients with PAH accounted for 13% in 1990 and 2% in 2007 [ ]. From January 1995 to June 2018, only 1863 cases of idiopathic PAH and 978 cases of other causes of PH were registered in ISHLT, accounting for only 2.9% and 1.5% of all transplant cases in the same period, respectively [ ]. The question is, where are the patients with PAH who are supposed to receive LTx? We should be aware that LTx may still be an underutilized treatment for PAH [ ]. Primarily, some patients may voluntarily forgo the LTx program for any number of reasons, whether religious beliefs or financial pressures. There are also some PAH patients with existing contraindications to transplantation, who are unable to derive a higher survival benefit from LTx. However, a more important consideration is the trade-off between adequate medical treatment and early referral for LTx in clinical practice [ , , ]. Specifically, since the introduction of targeted therapies such as epoprostenol, there have been significant improvements in hemodynamics, exercise capacity, and 5-year survival in patients with PAH [ , , ]. However, the disease course of PAH is unpredictable, and many patients receive effective medical treatment from the time of diagnosis, which results in a refusal of the LTx program. As the disease progresses, many patients become insensitive to medication and even continue to deteriorate rapidly [ ]. When patients with PAH are referred at the start of clinical deterioration, there may not be enough time to finish the assessment and obtain a suitable donor organ, and there is even a risk of death on the waiting list. Due to the expectation of medical treatment, physicians may fall into the “trap” of optimized medical treatment, neglecting early referrals for LTx in the course of PAH and ending with the patient missing the transplantation window [ , ]. These conditions may be more

When patients with PAH are referred at the start of clinical deterioration, there may not be enough time to finish the assessment and obtain a suitable donor organ, and there is even a risk of death on the waiting list. Due to the expectation of medical treatment, physicians may fall into the “trap” of optimized medical treatment, neglecting early referrals for LTx in the course of PAH and ending with the patient missing the transplantation window [ , ]. These conditions may be more troublesome in physicians coming from non-PH centers. Given the complexity of PAH management, physicians in primary-care centers should conduct a comprehensive assessment of patients with PAH, starting by predicting the disease progression according to the patient’s physical condition and risk factors, and formulating reasonable medical treatment strategies. Depending on the effectiveness of the medical intervention, patients could be referred to a superior medical facility with a PH center for the foreseeable future. 4.2. Referral Time Strategies In order to resolve the dilemma of LTx referral or even listing in patient populations with PAH, the 2014 ISHLT consensus document recommended referral for LTx when advanced symptoms or rapidly progressive disease were present despite an escalation of therapy [ ]. It is not hard to recognize that a previous LTx program is the “ultimate lifeline” after failed medical treatment. However, our brief is that “ultimate lifeline” does not equate to “only decide at the last minute”, that is, an LTx referral for patients with PAH should be performed as early as possible to cope with deteriorating conditions [ , , , ]. In the era of risk-assessment-based treatment, risk stratification of patients with PAH is particularly significant. Under the previous treatment algorithms, physicians relied more on diagnosis and treatment procedures than objective risk stratification, which led to a serious underestimation of prognostic risk in those patients [ , ]. According to REVEAL risk calculator 2.0 and the 2015 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines risk table, the sixth WSPH in 2018 indicated that patients with PAH at all risk levels who failed to reach low-risk status after 3–6 months of initial treatment required intensive treatment. If low-risk status has not been achieved after 3–6 months of maximum treatment, then patients should be referred for LTx evaluation [ ]. The 2021 ISHLT consensus document was introduced, the core content of which was that after adequate drug therapy, patients with intermediate or high risk based on the 2015 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines risk table or REVEAL risk score ≥ 8 should be considered for LTx referral [ ]. Interestingly, the latest 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines further revolutionized the 2015 ESC/ERS risk stratification model and also presented a new consensus on LTx referral timing for PAH. However, the applicability of this modified model needs to be validated by more prospective studies [ , ] ( ). Additional clinical data need to be considered during risk assessments, including cardiopulmonary exercise tests and right ventricular assessment by echocardiogram and/or cMRI, as well as specific clinical conditions known to be equivalent to high risks, such as renal dysfunction, liver dysfunction, pulmonary veno-occlusive disease/pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis (PVOD/PCH), connective-tissue-disease-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension, etc. [ , , , ]. Some evidence suggests that morbidity and mortality from PAH are driven by the influence of pulmonary hemodynamic dysfunction on renal dysfunction. In a REVEAL registry analysis, a ≥10% decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) for more than 1 year was an independent predictor of poorer survival in patients with PAH [ , ]. The balance between nephrotoxic immunosuppressive drugs and renal function after LTx is also complex and needs to be carefully evaluated at transplant referral. In addition, the main circulatory disturbances affecting liver function are congestion from right heart failure and ischemic injury from a low-cardiac-output state, which can be a serious consequence of severe PAH [ ]. Impaired synthetic liver function and decreased albumin levels were also shown in multiple studies to be strong independent predictors of poor outcomes in patients with PAH [ , ]. Although transplant referrals are too aggressive for moderate-risk patients, given that LTx presents unique challenges in patients with PAH, we should recognize the need for early referral in this population [ ]. It is worth mentioning that patients such as PVOD that are known to respond poorly to medical treatment should be referred promptly [ , ]. Patients with POVD/PCH may have a higher risk of dying on the waiting list compared to patients with PAH in the era of lung allocation. An analysis from the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) database showed that 22.6% of patients with PVOD died on the LTx waiting list, compared to 11% of patients with PAH at 6 months [

It is worth mentioning that patients such as PVOD that are known to respond poorly to medical treatment should be referred promptly [ , ]. Patients with POVD/PCH may have a higher risk of dying on the waiting list compared to patients with PAH in the era of lung allocation. An analysis from the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) database showed that 22.6% of patients with PVOD died on the LTx waiting list, compared to 11% of patients with PAH at 6 months [ ]. Therefore, given the limited options and the severity of this disease, an early referral for LTx is recommended as soon as POVD/PCH is diagnosed. In addition, it is recommended to closely monitor disease progression and apply for additional transplant priority for such patients when appropriate. The same is true for scleroderma, although LTx is currently rare in patients with scleroderma, which accounts for only 1.1% of all LTx [ ]. There is concern that the complex and severe extra-pulmonary manifestations of scleroderma may further reduce survival after LTx. However, recent studies have shown that post-transplant survival and chronic allograft lung dysfunction in patients with scleroderma are comparable to patients with other indications [ ]. Therefore, early referral for patients with scleroderma is also warranted [ ]. 4.3. Additional Benefits of Early Referral For patients in the high-risk group, either during initial treatment or optimized treatment, medical treatment and referral for LTx evaluation could theoretically be performed simultaneously [ ], which was reflected in the treatment algorithms from the sixth WSPH, but not covered by the latest 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines [ , , ]. We need to fully recognize that early referral does not mean early listing, but rather giving patients a tentative and comprehensive assessment, promoting transplant education, and addressing risk factors or potential causes of ineligibility for LTx in advance, such as obesity, infection, psychological problems, etc. Once the clinical condition deteriorates, the LTx listing can be performed in a timely manner [ , , , ]. In addition, an early referral may improve a patient’s chances of surviving to transplantation and reduce disease severity at the time of transplantation, and those whose physical condition worsens during the waiting period due to delayed referral and listing may have lower postoperative survival and quality of life even if the LTx is successful [ ]. The proposal for early referral upended the notion of passive waiting on the waiting list, giving patients with PAH the opportunity to use the waiting time to proactively complete more transplant-related preparations. 5. LTx Listing Time for Patients with PAH 5.1. Listing Time Referred patients with PAH will be formally evaluated for LTx eligibility, which involves routine indications and contraindications [ ]. This is a multidisciplinary process that must consider the overall clinical conditions of patients with PAH, including disease severity, psychological state, compliance, etc., which also means striking a balance between “patients who are severe enough” and “patients who are still in time for LTx”. Thus, it was indirectly demonstrated that early referral was beneficial for patients to be given sufficient time for a full assessment [ , ]. The risk stratification of patients with PAH is also tightly associated with the listing, and when patients show a high risk of short-term death, the listing should be considered despite optimized medical treatment [ , ]. Previously, LTx listing for patients with PAH was mostly based on the 2014 ISHLT consensus document, while the rapid development of risk stratification tools has brought more objectivity to this listing decision [ , ]. Based on these tools, the 2021 ISHLT consensus document has adjusted the listing criteria to the following: (1) ESC/ERS high-risk or REVEAL risk score >10 on appropriate PAH therapy, including IV or SC prostacyclin analogs; (2) progressive hypoxemia, especially in patients with PVOD or PCH; (3) progressive, but not end-stage, liver or kidney dysfunction due to PAH; and (4) life-threatening hemoptysis 24 (100%) [ ]. As mentioned above, the risk stratification of patients with PAH saw a breakthrough in the 2022 ESC/ERS PH guidelines, but the translation of this breakthrough into clinical practice needs to be validated by more in-depth studies. It is clear that all current efforts toward risk stratification are aimed at enabling a more objective assessment of the severity of PAH to facilitate successful referral and listing. However, early referral does not mean blind early listing under any circumstances. Patients with PAH should not be actively placed on the waiting list until all other available treatment options have been exhausted, as LTx itself is also a high-risk procedure, so transplant surgeons need to prudently evaluate the risks and benefits of LTx [ ] ( ). 5.2. Allocation of Donor Lung

However, early referral does not mean blind early listing under any circumstances. Patients with PAH should not be actively placed on the waiting list until all other available treatment options have been exhausted, as LTx itself is also a high-risk procedure, so transplant surgeons need to prudently evaluate the risks and benefits of LTx [ ] ( ). 5.2. Allocation of Donor Lung If patients with PAH meet the criteria and are on an active waiting list, there are policies in place to determine the patients’ priority relative to other candidates [ ]. In the early days, this priority was mainly based on the cumulative time a patient spent on the waiting list, but it was unfavorable to patients whose condition deteriorated faster [ ]. In 2005, the lung allocation score (LAS) was introduced to identify LTx priority according to the composite scores associated with the underlying disease severity, rate of clinical decline, and risk of death on the waiting list [ , ]. The LTx rates and waiting times for almost all end-stage lung diseases benefited from the LAS, effectively addressing the problem of the high mortality rate on the waiting list. However, the LTx rates for patients with PAH remain lower compared to other diagnoses, and mortality on PAH waiting lists is increasing, suggesting that LAS may be significantly underestimating the risk of death in patients with PAH [ , , , ]. In order to assess disease severity and mortality in PAH more accurately, various proposals led to a revision of the LAS algorithms in 2015, including reduced cardiac index and 6MWD, and increased resting oxygen consumption, creatinine, and bilirubin [ , , ]. For those patients whose calculated LAS score may not adequately reflect the urgency of and expected outcome after LTx, some regions allowed for an exceptional LAS to be given higher priority [ , ]. In addition, some proposals for urgent LTx, such as the high-priority allocation protocol introduced in France, have also significantly reduced the mortality on waiting lists in patients with PH [ ]. Specifically, urgent LTx is a prioritized allocation strategy for donor LTx according to the urgency of diseases, aiming to shorten the waiting time for donor lungs and reduce the fatality rate of patients on the waiting list for LTx [ ]. However, the specific protocols and standards for urgent LTx are not completely unified, and the boundaries between urgent strategies and the classic LAS system are blurred. The urgent LTx quotas in various countries ranged from 8.3% to 28% [ , , , ]. Interestingly, transplant centers in Spain do not strictly limit the fixed quota of urgent LTxs whose indications only included invasive mechanical ventilation and severe PAH, and those patients with severe PAH who underwent an urgent LTx had a more optimistic prognosis trend [ ]. The introduction of the concept of urgent LTx has provided new insights into LTx in patients with severe PAH, encouraging more attempts at allocation in this rapidly progressive disease. Objectively, high waiting list mortality should not be entirely blamed on the allocation system, as some patients with PAH are actually in a very critical state before the listing, which also indirectly proves the importance of early referral [ ]. Therefore, we should take an objective attitude to the listing of patients with PAH and evaluate it according to the severity and risk of the disease. Patients who deteriorate rapidly in a short period deserve more attention and priority. However, blind premature listing can conflict with transplant priorities, significantly lengthening waiting time and leading to an increase in unnecessary waiting list deaths. As mentioned above, advanced medication therapy can be performed at the same time as an LTx referral, which does not imply a definite possibility of listing. When patients with PAH become relatively stable during evaluation without obvious organ failure, or reversible factors and poor psychological adherence occur, physicians could terminate the LTx referral and listing and closely monitor the disease progression in order to reactivate the evaluation procedure if the conditions worsen. 6. However, medical management is particularly challenging in severe PAH patients due to alterations in medication pharmacokinetics resulting from end-stage organ damage [ ]. order to reactivate the evaluation procedure if the conditions worsen. 6. Other Management on the Waiting List When a patient with PAH is placed on the LTx waiting list, medical treatment for PAH ought to continue, aiming to prepare the patient for LTx and to perform at peak condition [ , ]. However, medical management is particularly challenging in severe PAH patients due to alterations in medication pharmacokinetics resulting from end-stage organ damage [ ]. In addition to the prescribing of epoprostenol, volume management and positive inotropic drugs are equally important, given that the increased afterload in the pulmonary circulation leads to right ventricle remodeling and ultimately failure through various mechanisms [ , ]. Volume management in patients with PAH includes managing diuretic use and electrolyte imbalance, as well as monitoring fluid retention due to the use of endothelin receptor antagonists or calcium channel blockers [ ]. Briefly, pre-transplant management is a multidisciplinary, collaborative procedure, so it is critical to establish close collaboration between PAH physicians and transplant surgeons. In addition, for many eligible patients, bridging strategies may be required to keep patients alive while on the waiting list and avoid irreversible end-organ damage [ ]. The risk of death from PAH is total heart failure due to progression of right heart failure, and cardiac arrest secondary to arrhythmia. In order to transition medical treatment to a successful LTx, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) can act as an important bridging strategy [ , , ]. Previous studies have shown that ECMO can increase the survival rate and decrease the incidence of postoperative complications when compared to cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) [ , ]. The specific strategies of ECMO for LTx in PAH patients should be developed by a multidisciplinary team of pulmonologists, intensivists, surgeons, and ECMO specialists. Even though venovenous ECMO (VV-ECMO) has multiple clinical advantages in terms of the operation and associated risk, a low risk of bleeding, and less anticoagulation, it is usually not suitable in PAH patients because VV-ECMO requires the patient’s right ventricle to function as the system’s pump [ ]. Distinctively, in the presence of an atrial septal defect or a large patent foramen ovale, VV-ECMO can be inserted into the right internal jugular vein using a double-lumen catheter, so as to inject returned blood directly into the atrial septum to form an oxygenated right-to-left shunt [ ]. However, as soon as heart function deteriorates in PAH patients, urgent conversion to VA-ECMO is required. VA-ECMO is a commonly used option that bypasses the original high-resistance pulmonary circulation, reduces the right ventricular load, and delivers oxygenated blood directly to the systemic circulation to improve end-stage organ function [ ]. In a study of interstitial lung disease patients with PH, the survival of LTx recipients in initial VA-ECMO was significantly higher than that in VV-ECMO, with a 59% lower risk of death compared to VV-ECMO [ ]. However, several serious complications limit the long-term use of ECMO, including hemolysis, intubation site bleeding, sepsis, cerebrovascular accidents, and multiple organ failure [ ]. In addition, Fischer et al. introduced the application of a Novalung pumpless lung assist device with conduits (Novalung LAD), which can be considered as a bridge to LTx or HLT [ , , ]. The Novalung device connects a low-resistance diffusion membrane parallel with the pulmonary artery to the left atrium (PA-LA). The inherent right ventricular cardiac output drives blood flow through a low-resistance diffusion membrane, where blood is oxygenated and returned to the systemic circulation without pumping [ , ]. Compared to VA-ECMO, PA-LA Novalung has allowed a reduction in inotrope support, an improvement in gas exchange parameters, optimization of ventilatory support requirements and extubation in selected cases, prolonged cardiopulmonary support, and recovery of right ventricular function [ ]. For patients with PAH who cannot receive mechanical circulatory support to bridge to LTx, balloon atrial septostomy (BAS) or the Potts shunt could be considered [ , , ]. BAS is a procedure that uses balloon dilation to create an atrial shunt through a right cardiac catheter to achieve right ventricular decompression and improve cardiac output by increasing the left ventricular preload [ ]. However, the mortality associated with BAS is about 10%, and it is limited to symptomatic relief and emergency use [ ]. In extremely rare cases, when ECMO and BAS are contraindicated, the Potts shunt may be considered to decompress the right ventricle and bridge the patient for transplantation [ , ]. 7. Conclusions LTx remains the ultimate therapeutic option for patients with PAH who have failed to respond to maximum medical treatment. The LTx referral and listing serve as an extremely essential first step to performing this salvage surgery successfully. In recent years, the definition, classification, and risk stratification of PAH, as well as comprehensive treatment algorithms, have made radical progress. Physicians and transplant

In extremely rare cases, when ECMO and BAS are contraindicated, the Potts shunt may be considered to decompress the right ventricle and bridge the patient for transplantation [ , ]. 7. Conclusions LTx remains the ultimate therapeutic option for patients with PAH who have failed to respond to maximum medical treatment. The LTx referral and listing serve as an extremely essential first step to performing this salvage surgery successfully. In recent years, the definition, classification, and risk stratification of PAH, as well as comprehensive treatment algorithms, have made radical progress. Physicians and transplant surgeons should grasp this opportunity, continuously optimizing medical treatment algorithms, and dealing with LTx referral and listing by favoring early and objective assessments, respectively. For each patient with severe PAH, the risks and benefits must be prudently weighed to determine the most appropriate transplant strategy.

chunks.content: Introduction Cardiogenic shock (CS) is a life-threatening acute cardiac failure syndrome leading to persistent hypoperfusion, entailing short-term mortality of 30–40% and exceeding 50% at one year. While acute myocardial infarction remains a major cause, cases related to acute or acute-on-chronic heart failure (HF) have been on the rise, underscoring the heterogeneity of CS [ , , , ]. Recent advances include refined classifications such as the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) staging system, which effectively stratifies prognosis [ ] and guides management, and the growing adoption of multidisciplinary “shock teams” and regional networks. Though numerous position papers and reviews are published every year, the most recent specific international guidelines on management of CS regardless of the etiology were issued over 10 years ago [ , ]. Over the past decade, multiple studies have investigated CS and its symptomatic treatments, including inotropes and mechanical circulatory support, but most have yielded negative results [ , , , ]. In contrast, and despite the increasing performance of percutaneous interventions for severe valvular disease, randomized trials specifically addressing etiological management remain scarce [ ]. To address this gap, the French-Language Society of Intensive Care (Société de Réanimation de Langue Française (SRLF)) and the French Cardiology Society (SFC) convened a multidisciplinary task force to develop evidence-based recommendations using the Grading of Recommendation Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Twenty-three “Patient Intervention Comparator Outcome” (PICO) questions were identified across six domains of CS care, leading to 41 recommendations regarding management of CS in adult patients. These guidelines aim to provide an updated, pragmatic framework for clinicians managing this complex syndrome. Methodology Expert panel These guidelines focused on the management of CS in adult (≥18 years) patients. The guidelines were developed using the GRADE methodology by an expert committee comprising members of the SRLF and the SFC, with the participation of the French Society of Anesthesia and Intensive Care [Société Française d'Anesthésie et de Réanimation (SFAR)], and the French Society of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery [Société Française de Chirurgie Thoracique et Cardio-Vasculaire (SFCTCV)]. The various disciplines contributing to the management of CS in adults were represented as follows: cardiology, intensive care, anesthesia and cardiac surgery. Scope and definitions We included adult patients presenting with CS due to acute myocardial infarction and acute decompensated HF-CS (ischemic and non-ischemic). Neonates and pediatric patients were excluded. CS patients due to pulmonary embolism (according to the recent European Society of Cardiology [ESC] guidelines) [ ], endocarditis (according to the recent ESC guidelines) [ ], myocarditis (according the recent ESC guidelines [ ], mixed shock post-cardiac arrest, septic cardiomyopathy, shock following cardiac surgery and drug intoxication were excluded. Methods Key questions were identified by the organizing committee. They were formulated in a Patient Intervention Comparator Outcome (PICO) format following an initial meeting of the expert group. The PICO questions defined the scope of the literature search. The task force of experts also defined keywords for literature searches, determined the time frame for these searches, identified the target populations, and specified the specific outcomes to be addressed [ ]. The literature was analyzed using the GRADE methodology [ ]. Initially, a level of evidence was assigned to each bibliographic reference based on study design and methodological quality. Subsequently, an overall level of evidence was determined among the experts for each PICO question according to the GRADE methodology. The GRADE process distinctly separates evaluation of the quality of evidence from the strength of the recommendation statements. This separation allows for incorporation of the balance of the risks and benefits associated with adoption of the recommendation. Consequently, even with relatively weak evidence, a recommendation can be deemed “strong” if the net benefits outweighed the harms. A high overall level of evidence (GRADE 1+: should be used, treated, done/ GRADE 1-: should not be) led to a “strong” recommendation. A moderate level of evidence resulted in a “moderate” recommendation (GRADE 2+: should probably/ GRADE 2-: should probably not). When the literature was insufficient or nonexistent, expert opinion was used to formulate recommendations (experts suggest or can be). The proposed recommendations were presented and discussed at two expert meetings. Each expert rated each recommendation on a scale ranging from 1 (complete disagreement) to 9 (complete agreement). All experts voted on recommendations. The collective rating was established using a GRADE grid methodology. To approve a recommendation, at least 50% of the experts had to agree, and fewer than 20% could disagree. For strong agreement, at least 70% of the experts had to agree. If strong agreement was not achieved, the recommendations were revised and re-rated to reach consensus. The wording of all recommendations strictly followed the predefined GRADE-based methodology. In this framework, the use of terms such as ‘should’ versus ‘should probably’ directly reflects the strength of the recommendation and the level of evidence, with ‘should
