The first study was almost 3 decades ago and evaluated only 19 donors. They found that among 8 donors with elevated cardiac troponin I values, 5 (63%) experienced graft failure. The second study is also more than a decade old and included information for 657 donors. This study evaluated only the last available troponin value and found no association between the final troponin values and graft failure. In a clinical setting, the 2 factors more often deliberated on are the peak donor troponin value and, more importantly, the trend of these values over time. Often, clinicians ask that donor troponin values be repeated to ensure that there is improvement, with the assumption that this correlates with recovery of the myocardium following the event that led to the donor’s demise. An important finding from our national study that evaluated over 4500 donors is that after adjusting for donor and recipient confounders, peak donor troponin value does affect graft outcome for pediatric HT recipients. As noted in this study, recipients of donor hearts with peak troponin levels at the 75th percentile (0.66 ng/mL) exhibited a 22% increased risk of graft loss within the first year after HT compared with recipients of donor hearts with troponin levels at the 25th percentile (0.04 ng/mL). These findings suggest that HT clinicians should exercise caution when considering donor hearts with peak troponin concentrations exceeding 0.66 ng/mL. It is important to mention that, in this study, after adjusting for all other confounders, ejection fraction was not a significant contributor to worse post‐HT graft survival. These findings are similar to a previous multicenter analysis among adult HT recipients, where the authors found that recipients receiving donor hearts with borderline ejection fraction (40%–50%) or reduced ejection fraction (<40%) had similar 1‐year survival to recipients who received donor hearts with normal ejection fraction (≥50%). In this study, post‐HT graft survival for recipients of donors with increasing or persistently high donor troponin values were similar to those with low or decreasing values over time. The authors did not have information as to when the troponin values were collected relative to the time of brain death. It is known that catecholamine levels are highest in the first hour after brain death, and this is when cardiac contractility is most often impaired. , Hence, it is valuable for donor hospitals to collect troponin values at this time, as that may be reflective of peak values that clinicians can then use as they consider donor organ acceptance. Other important findings of this study are the donor and recipient characteristics associated with an elevated troponin. As has been shown in the adult study, we also found donors with elevated troponin to more likely have received cardiopulmonary resuscitation. However, in contrast with the adult study, in our study, donors with elevated troponin levels were more likely to have associated left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Pediatric programs tend to accept donors with elevated troponins for recipients who are sicker, and this may partly be due to the concerns for accepting such donors for otherwise stable recipients. This finding contrasts with adults, where such donors are accepted for patients who are not sicker. We did not find any association between donor troponin trends and graft outcomes. More specifically, post‐HT graft survival for donors with increasing or persistently high donor troponin values were similar to those with low or decreasing values over time. The study findings will be valuable to clinicians and reduce the time and effort by organ procurement organizations, as they often must delay donor operating room time as they are trying to obtain and report repeat troponin values at the recipient institution’s request. Limitations This study has inherent limitations secondary to the use of a national registry for research. It is important to note that, in our study, most pediatric recipients (93.6%) accepted for HT had normal left ventricular function. Given the low number of patients with left ventricular systolic dysfunction, we were unable to determine if an elevated or rising troponin value in those with systolic dysfunction may lead to worse outcomes. We suspect that the reason why left ventricular systolic dysfunction was not a significant risk factor for post‐HT death is the time course of the dysfunction early after brain death. Left ventricular systolic dysfunction occurring early after brain death may not significantly affect post‐HT outcomes, but if it remains persistently low despite donor optimization, caution will need to be exercised in accepting

had normal left ventricular function. Given the low number of patients with left ventricular systolic dysfunction, we were unable to determine if an elevated or rising troponin value in those with systolic dysfunction may lead to worse outcomes. We suspect that the reason why left ventricular systolic dysfunction was not a significant risk factor for post‐HT death is the time course of the dysfunction early after brain death. Left ventricular systolic dysfunction occurring early after brain death may not significantly affect post‐HT outcomes, but if it remains persistently low despite donor optimization, caution will need to be exercised in accepting such hearts. We included only pediatric patients who ultimately underwent HT. HT clinicians thoroughly assess donor–recipient suitability before acceptance. Hence, no comments could be made for donors with elevated troponin who ultimately were not accepted on the basis of this analysis. Conclusions Most pediatric recipients receive hearts from donors with abnormal troponin values. Donors with elevated troponin are more likely to have received resuscitation and have lower left ventricular systolic function. Recipients who receive donor hearts with elevated troponins are often sicker than those who receive donor hearts with normal troponin values. Higher peak donor troponin values (>0.66 ng/mL) were significantly associated with worse 1‐year post‐HT graft survival. However, after adjusting donor and recipient characteristics, neither a persistently elevated donor troponin value nor an increasing donor troponin value leads to worse post‐HT outcomes. Further research is needed to understand the impact of elevated troponins in those with persistent left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Sources of Funding None. Disclosures S.A. is site principal investigator for a multicenter study led by the University of Michigan and site principal investigator for the FUEL‐2 (Fontan Udenafil Exercise Longitudinal Assessment Trial) study (Mezzion) and reports no salary support. M.T. is site principal investigator for the VALOR (Vericiguat in Pediatric Participants With Heart Failure Due to Systemic Left Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction) heart failure trial (Merck) and reports no salary support. The remaining authors have no disclosures to report. Supporting information Table S1 Figures S1–S3

chunks.content: Introduction Cardiometabolic disease has emerged as the leading cause of death beyond the first year after heart transplantation, accounting for 30%−40% of late mortality. , , Post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM) develops in 30%−40% of recipients within 12 months and confers a 2-fold increased risk of cardiac allograft vasculopathy and mortality. , , Chronic kidney disease (CKD), present in over 50% of recipients by year 5, progresses to end-stage renal disease requiring dialysis or re-transplantation in 10–20% of patients. Obesity affects an increasing proportion of recipients and contributes to hypertension, dyslipidemia, and graft dysfunction. Contemporary guidelines emphasize aggressive management of modifiable cardiometabolic risk factors as a cornerstone of long-term post-transplant care. Current therapies for PTDM often require complex regimens and may be associated with weight gain or limited weight loss. In the general population, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) improve glycemic control and weight and have demonstrated cardiovascular and kidney benefits in large, randomized trials, leading to guideline endorsement for patients with type 2 diabetes, obesity, CKD, and cardiovascular disease. , , , , , , , Despite this evidence, heart transplant recipients were excluded from pivotal GLP-1 RA trials due to concerns about gastrointestinal intolerance, altered absorption, and potential interactions with calcineurin inhibitors. , , , The extent to which GLP-1 RAs may affect tacrolimus or cyclosporine absorption, immunosuppression adequacy, or rejection risk remains incompletely characterized in the transplant population. Small studies in kidney and liver transplantation suggest GLP-1 RAs may improve metabolic parameters without destabilizing calcineurin-inhibitor levels or increasing rejection risk, but these findings cannot be directly extrapolated to heart transplant recipients. , , , However, heart transplant recipients differ fundamentally due to their unique hemodynamics, higher rejection vigilance, and different immunosuppression intensity, precluding direct extrapolation. No comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis have specifically evaluated the effects of GLP-1 RAs in adult heart transplant recipients. We hypothesized that GLP-1 RA therapy would be associated with improved cardiometabolic profiles. The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to consolidate available evidence regarding the metabolic, renal, and safety outcomes of GLP-1 RA therapy in adult heart transplant recipients. Methods Study design and reporting standards This systematic review and meta-analysis followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. A prespecified protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251243172) before study initiation. Eligibility criteria Population Adults (≥18 years) who underwent orthotopic heart transplantation and received any GLP-1 receptor agonist post-transplant for type 2 diabetes, obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²), or cardiometabolic risk reduction. Outcomes Primary outcomes were change in body mass index (BMI, kg/m²) and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c, %) from baseline to ≥3 months follow-up. Secondary outcomes included body weight, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), triglycerides, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and insulin requirements. Safety outcomes included acute rejection, calcineurin inhibitor dose adjustments, gastrointestinal adverse events, and treatment discontinuations. Study design We included observational comparative cohorts, case-control studies, and single-group pre-post intervention studies with ≥5 participants reporting quantitative outcomes. Randomized trials were eligible a priori, but none met the inclusion criteria. Exclusions included case reports, studies without extractable heart transplant data, and non-English language publications. Mixed solid-organ transplant studies including heart transplant recipients were eligible but only used as indirect evidence unless they reported heart-specific data. Search strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Scopus from inception through January 31, 2025. Search strategies incorporated controlled vocabulary (MeSH, Emtree) and keywords including: (GLP-1 OR semaglutide OR liraglutide OR dulaglutide OR tirzepatide OR exenatide) AND (heart transplant OR cardiac transplant). The reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews were screened using backward and forward citation tracking. Study selection and data extraction Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts, with discrepancies resolved through discussion or third-reviewer adjudication. The selection process is summarized in a PRISMA flow diagram ( ). Data were extracted using a standardized form that included study design, sample size, participant characteristics, GLP-1 receptor agonist type and dose, follow-up duration, co-interventions/confounders (including concomitant SGLT2 inhibitor exposure when reported), and outcomes. For mixed solid-organ transplant studies, only outcomes explicitly reported for heart transplant recipients were extracted for heart-specific synthesis. If an endpoint could not be isolated to the heart-transplant subgroup, that study contributed only to the qualitative review for that endpoint. For continuous outcomes, mean changes and standard deviations (or 95% CIs) were extracted. When unavailable, standard deviations were calculated from CIs, standard errors, or t-statistics. Risk of bias assessment Two reviewers independently assessed risk of bias using the ROBINS-I tool because all included studies were non-randomized ( ). Domains included confounding, selection, intervention classification, missing data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or third-reviewer adjudication. Statistical analysis Meta-analyses were performed using the metafor package (version 4.8–0) in R (version 4.5.0). Random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood (REML)

contributed only to the qualitative review for that endpoint. For continuous outcomes, mean changes and standard deviations (or 95% CIs) were extracted. When unavailable, standard deviations were calculated from CIs, standard errors, or t-statistics. Risk of bias assessment Two reviewers independently assessed risk of bias using the ROBINS-I tool because all included studies were non-randomized ( ). Domains included confounding, selection, intervention classification, missing data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or third-reviewer adjudication. Statistical analysis Meta-analyses were performed using the metafor package (version 4.8–0) in R (version 4.5.0). Random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation were used for outcomes reported by ≥2 studies with sufficiently similar heart-transplant-specific outcome definitions. Continuous outcomes were summarized as mean differences with 95% CIs. Pre-post analyses used change-from-baseline estimates. Between-group comparisons from comparative cohorts were not pooled with pre-post data. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic and the Cochran Q test, p < 0.10 indicated significant heterogeneity. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were conducted for all pooled outcomes to assess the influence of individual studies on effect estimates. Prespecified subgroup analyses were planned but not performed because of the limited number of studies. Sparse safety data, including rejection events and immunosuppressant dose changes, were synthesized descriptively rather than quantitatively. Because one included study reported pooled outcomes for a mixed solid-organ cohort that included heart transplant recipients, these estimates were considered indirect evidence when incorporated into the synthesis. Formal assessment of publication bias using funnel plots and Egger's regression test was not performed because fewer than 10 studies were available for each pooled outcome, limiting statistical power for bias detection. Sex was reported descriptively; sex-stratified analyses were not feasible due to limited data. Certainty of evidence The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework was used to assess the certainty of evidence for each primary and key secondary outcome. Each outcome was rated as high, moderate, or low certainty based on five domains: risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias ( ). Results Study selection The systematic search identified 725 records; 414 unique records remained after deduplication. Following title and abstract screening, 18 full-text articles underwent detailed assessment. Fourteen studies were excluded: 10 were conference abstracts without sufficient quantitative data, two had inappropriate study designs, one included an ineligible population, and one was a narrative review. Four studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis ( ). Study characteristics The included studies comprised three single-group pre–post cohorts , , and one matched retrospective cohort study. Studies were published between 2020 and 2024 and conducted in the United States (n = 3) and Israel (n = 1). Median follow-up ranged from 9 to 37 months. Two studies included mixed solid-organ transplant populations. For these studies, only heart-transplant subgroup data explicitly reported by the original authors were extracted for heart-specific summaries. Outcomes that could not be separated for heart recipients were excluded from pooled analyses. One study also included concomitant SGLT2 inhibitor exposure, which was captured as an important co-intervention and considered in the risk-of-bias assessment and interpretation. Among pre–post studies, GLP-1 receptor agonists were initiated a median of 3–5 years following heart transplantation. Semaglutide was the most frequently prescribed agent, followed by liraglutide and dulaglutide. Baseline prevalence of type 2 diabetes ranged from 60% to over 80%, and mean baseline body mass index ranged from 31 to 36 kg/m² ( ). Risk of Bias All included studies were observational and assessed using the ROBINS-I tool. Overall risk of bias ranged from moderate to serious, driven primarily by confounding, selection bias, absence of concurrent controls in pre-post studies, and co-interventions. Important potential confounders included baseline obesity and diabetes severity, time from transplant, concurrent glucose-lowering therapies such as SGLT2 inhibitors, steroid exposure, and changes in immunosuppression. The matched cohort study demonstrated lower overall risk of bias but remained susceptible to residual confounding despite propensity score matching ( ). Primary outcomes Body mass index Three pre-post studies reported BMI change data. Random-effects meta-analysis (k = 3) demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in BMI following GLP-1 RA initiation: Pooled mean difference: −2·24 kg/m² (95% CI −3·49 to −0·98; p = 0·0005) Moderate heterogeneity was observed (I² = 56.8%; Q (2) = 4.48, p = 0.106). Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the pooled estimate, with consistent direction and statistical significance across analyses. The observed heterogeneity appeared driven by differences in baseline obesity severity, GLP-1 receptor agonist selection, and follow-up duration. The matched cohort study reported a smaller, non-significant between-group difference in BMI. This finding was not pooled due to methodological heterogeneity but was directionally consistent ( ). Glycemic control Two pre-post studies reported HbA1c outcome data. Meta-analysis (k = 2) demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in HbA1c: Pooled mean difference: −0·62% points (95% CI −0·94 to

56.8%; Q (2) = 4.48, p = 0.106). Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the pooled estimate, with consistent direction and statistical significance across analyses. The observed heterogeneity appeared driven by differences in baseline obesity severity, GLP-1 receptor agonist selection, and follow-up duration. The matched cohort study reported a smaller, non-significant between-group difference in BMI. This finding was not pooled due to methodological heterogeneity but was directionally consistent ( ). Glycemic control Two pre-post studies reported HbA1c outcome data. Meta-analysis (k = 2) demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in HbA1c: Pooled mean difference: −0·62% points (95% CI −0·94 to −0·31; p = 0·0001) No heterogeneity was observed (I² = 0%; Q (1) = 0.11, p = 0.736), and sensitivity analyses demonstrated stable effect estimates. The matched cohort study similarly reported a significant between-group reduction in HbA1c favoring GLP-1 receptor agonist users. Secondary outcomes Body weight Two pre-post studies reported absolute body weight change. Random-effects meta-analysis (k = 2) demonstrated a statistically significant weight reduction : Pooled mean difference: −7·82 kg (95% CI −14·99 to −0·65; p = 0·032) Substantial heterogeneity was observed (I² = 71.3%; Q (1) = 3.49, p = 0.062), likely reflecting differences in baseline obesity, GLP-1 receptor agonist agent and dosing, duration of therapy, and intensity of concurrent lifestyle interventions. Despite heterogeneity, the direction of effect was consistent across studies. Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol Two pre-post studies reported LDL-C change. Meta-analysis (k = 2) demonstrated a statistically significant reduction: Pooled mean difference: −11·88 mg/dL (95% CI −22·85 to −0·91; p = 0·034) Low-to-moderate heterogeneity was observed (I² = 36.6%; Q (1) = 1.58, p = 0.209). The matched cohort study did not demonstrate a significant between-group difference in LDL cholesterol. Triglyceride outcomes were inconsistently reported and were not pooled. One study demonstrated a non-significant pre–post reduction, while the matched cohort study reported a significant between-group reduction favoring GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy. Renal function by estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) Renal outcomes were reported in a limited number of studies. One pre–post study evaluating estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) showed no significant change following initiation of a GLP-1 receptor agonist over approximately 12 months. Additional studies reported stable renal function, with no evidence of acute kidney injury or accelerated decline. Due to limited data and heterogeneous reporting, a meta-analysis of renal outcomes was not performed. Insulin requirements The magnitude of insulin reduction varied substantially, likely reflecting differences in baseline insulin resistance, concurrent medication use, and dietary interventions. Safety outcomes Immunosuppression management and graft rejection Safety data related to immunosuppression and graft outcomes were limited and inconsistently reported across studies. Tacrolimus levels were generally reported as stable when monitored after GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation. A small proportion of patients required calcineurin inhibitor dose adjustments, though none could be clearly attributable to initiation of GLP-1 receptor agonist. No study reported a clear increase in acute or chronic rejection temporally associated with GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy, although these events were sparsely reported and not systematically assessed. Also, rejection events were rare in the available reports. One acute rejection event was reported temporally following initiation in a single patient, though causality could not be established. Adverse events Gastrointestinal intolerance was the most commonly reported adverse event and accounted for the majority of treatment discontinuations. Overall discontinuation rates ranged from approximately 5% to 15%, consistent with rates observed in non-transplant populations. No study reported episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis, acute pancreatitis, or severe hypoglycemia directly attributable to GLP-1 RA therapy. No cases of acute kidney injury or sudden eGFR decline were documented. Thiyagarajan et al. evaluated thyroid nodules and malignancy surveillance but found no safety signals. Certainty of evidence assessment GRADE assessments evaluated the quality of evidence across five domains. Using the GRADE framework, certainty of evidence was rated as moderate for reductions in BMI and HbA1c, downgraded primarily due to observational study design. Certainty was rated as low for body weight and LDL cholesterol outcomes due to heterogeneity and imprecision, and very low for renal outcomes due to limited data. No outcomes were downgraded for indirectness, as all were directly relevant to post-transplant care, or for publication bias, as assessment was not feasible with <10 studies , ( ). Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis is, to our knowledge, the first to synthesize the available evidence in adult heart transplant recipients. Across a small and methodologically limited observational literature, our findings demonstrate that GLP-1 RA therapy is associated with clinically meaningful improvements in cardiometabolic parameters. These findings align with the established efficacy of GLP-1 RAs in non-transplant populations. , , , , , However, conclusions regarding graft-related safety and immunosuppressant interactions should be drawn with caution, as these outcomes were reported inconsistently. Key findings GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with significant reductions in BMI (pooled mean −2.24 kg/m²) and HbA1c (−0.62% points), corresponding

and meta-analysis is, to our knowledge, the first to synthesize the available evidence in adult heart transplant recipients. Across a small and methodologically limited observational literature, our findings demonstrate that GLP-1 RA therapy is associated with clinically meaningful improvements in cardiometabolic parameters. These findings align with the established efficacy of GLP-1 RAs in non-transplant populations. , , , , , However, conclusions regarding graft-related safety and immunosuppressant interactions should be drawn with caution, as these outcomes were reported inconsistently. Key findings GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with significant reductions in BMI (pooled mean −2.24 kg/m²) and HbA1c (−0.62% points), corresponding to approximately 7–10 kg weight loss in the post-transplant setting. Even modest weight reduction has been associated with improvements in blood pressure, insulin sensitivity, and functional capacity in transplant recipients, and may mitigate the progression of obesity-related complications. , , , , , It also resulted in consistent and significant improvement in glycemic control, with a pooled reduction in hemoglobin A1c of 0.62% points and no observed heterogeneity. This magnitude of glycemic improvement is comparable to that observed in non-transplant populations and is relevant given the high prevalence of post-transplant diabetes mellitus and its association with adverse cardiovascular and graft-related outcomes. , , Several studies reported reduced insulin requirements, with some patients discontinuing insulin entirely. , , , , Reported safety outcomes were limited. Across the included studies, tacrolimus levels generally remained stable when monitored, and some patients required calcineurin inhibitor dose adjustments. However, these reports were based on small sample sizes, were not uniformly collected, and could not establish causality. Gastrointestinal intolerance and treatment discontinuation were the most consistently described adverse effects and were similar to those observed in non-transplant populations. , , , , , The metabolic benefits observed appear comparable to those in non-transplant populations, though absolute reductions were smaller, likely reflecting the transplant population's baseline comorbidity burden and physical activity limitations. , , , Emerging data from kidney and liver transplant recipients similarly show metabolic improvements without an obvious signal of immunosuppression destabilization, although those studies are likewise observational. , The present analysis extends these observations to heart transplant recipients, and should be viewed as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive. The consistency of glycemic and weight effects across transplant and non-transplant populations suggests that the efficacy of GLP-1 RAs is not meaningfully attenuated by immunosuppressive therapy. However, the observational nature of transplant studies precludes definitive comparison to randomized controlled trials. Safety and immunosuppression considerations A key concern among transplant recipients is whether GLP-1 RAs alter the absorption of concurrent immunosuppressants due to delayed gastric emptying. , In the heart-transplant studies included here, evidence addressing this question was limited to small observational reports. 5–7% of transplant recipients in observational studies required dose adjustments attributable to initiation of GLP-1 RA. Tacrolimus levels remained generally stable across studies, and dose changes could have reflected routine clinical adjustment rather than a drug-drug interaction. Gastrointestinal adverse events led to discontinuation in approximately 5–10% of patients, consistent with discontinuation rates in non-transplant populations receiving GLP-1 RA therapy. Likewise, because rejection events were rare and follow-up was limited, the current literature is insufficient to exclude modest but clinically meaningful effects on rejection risk or graft function. Accordingly, our findings should not be interpreted as proving immunologic safety. Rather, the available studies did not identify a consistent signal of frequent short-term harm, while remaining underpowered to detect uncommon graft-related events. Longer-term prospective studies with prespecified monitoring of tacrolimus exposure, rejection, and graft function are required before firm conclusions can be drawn. Renal outcomes Renal dysfunction is highly prevalent after heart transplantation and represents a major determinant of long-term morbidity and mortality. , In the present analysis, renal outcomes were reported inconsistently and could not be pooled. Available data demonstrated a stable estimated glomerular filtration rate following GLP-1 RA initiation, with no signal for accelerated decline or acute kidney injury. While large trials in non-transplant populations have demonstrated renoprotective effects, current evidence in heart transplant recipients supports renal safety rather than benefit. Dedicated prospective studies with kidney-specific endpoints are needed. Clinical implications Despite the observational nature of the available data, these findings have important implications for clinical practice. GLP-1 receptor agonists appear to be a reasonable therapeutic option for stable heart transplant recipients with post-transplant diabetes mellitus, obesity, or inadequate glycemic control on conventional therapies. Given the observed metabolic benefits and the absence of a consistent short-term harm signal in limited observational data, GLP-1 RAs may be considered in selected stable heart transplant recipients with careful clinical and immunosuppressant monitoring. Patients most likely to benefit may include those who are more than one-year post-transplant with stable graft function, established diabetes or obesity, and preserved renal function. Agent selection should be individualized based on indication, tolerability, dosing frequency, and insurance coverage. Knowledge gaps and future directions Prospective

therapeutic option for stable heart transplant recipients with post-transplant diabetes mellitus, obesity, or inadequate glycemic control on conventional therapies. Given the observed metabolic benefits and the absence of a consistent short-term harm signal in limited observational data, GLP-1 RAs may be considered in selected stable heart transplant recipients with careful clinical and immunosuppressant monitoring. Patients most likely to benefit may include those who are more than one-year post-transplant with stable graft function, established diabetes or obesity, and preserved renal function. Agent selection should be individualized based on indication, tolerability, dosing frequency, and insurance coverage. Knowledge gaps and future directions Prospective randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm the metabolic benefits of GLP-1 RAs in heart transplant recipients and to evaluate effects on cardiovascular events, cardiac allograft vasculopathy, graft survival, and mortality. Longer-term follow-up studies are essential to assess the durability of benefit and late safety signals. Prospective pharmacokinetic studies evaluating interactions between GLP-1 RAs and immunosuppressive agents would provide mechanistic insight and inform optimal dosing strategies. Future studies should also explore whether treatment effects vary by GLP-1 RA agent, time since transplant, baseline renal function, or degree of metabolic disease. Finally, real-world implementation studies examining adherence, cost-effectiveness, and patient-reported outcomes will be critical to guide widespread adoption in transplant care. Limitations All included studies were observational, with inherent susceptibility to selection bias, confounding by indication, and co-intervention bias. Pre-post designs lacked control groups, and residual confounding cannot be excluded. Two studies included mixed solid-organ transplant populations, and our review relied on heart-transplant subgroup data only when these were explicitly reported; incomplete subgroup reporting may have limited certainty for some endpoints. One study included concomitant exposure to an SGLT2 inhibitor, which may have contributed to the observed metabolic changes. Sample sizes were small, follow-up was limited, and outcome reporting was heterogeneous. Publication bias assessment was underpowered. Certainty of evidence was moderate for BMI and HbA1c. Safety outcomes were sparsely reported and not suitable for pooling. Data regarding weight rebound after discontinuation of GLP-1 RA therapy were not systematically reported. Sex-specific analyses were not feasible. Conclusion In this systematic review and meta-analysis, GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy was associated with improved weight and glycemic control in adult heart transplant recipients. Renal function appeared stable in the limited available reports. Current observational data did not identify a consistent short-term signal of harm related to immunosuppression management or graft outcomes, but the evidence is insufficient to establish safety with confidence. These findings suggest that GLP-1 RAs may represent a potentially useful adjunctive therapy for cardiometabolic management after heart transplantation. Prospective, adequately powered trials are needed before GLP-1 RAs can be definitively recommended as standard-of-care therapy in this population. Ethics and transplant declaration This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of previously published data. All included studies were conducted in accordance with institutional and national ethical standards and complied with the Declaration of Helsinki. The authors affirm that no organs or tissues were procured from executed prisoners or prisoners of conscience, and that donor consent and organ procurement procedures adhered to internationally accepted ethical guidelines, including the Declaration of Istanbul and ISHLT transplant ethics policies. No AI tools were used for data analysis, result interpretation, or the generation of scientific content. All authors reviewed and approved the final manuscript and take full responsibility for its accuracy and integrity. chunks.content: Introduction Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) are classically defined as a heterogeneous group of diseases primarily characterized by the common feature of immune-mediated inflammation of muscle fibers and surrounding tissues. The annual incidence of IIM ranges from 0.2 to 2 per 100,000 person-years, with a prevalence ranging from 2 to 25 per 100,000 people. However, these systemic diseases can manifest with a combination of inflammatory muscle, skin, lung, and joint disease. Using clinical features, serology, and muscle pathology, currently, six main phenotypes have been described in adults. Each phenotype has a distinct typical presentation. ( ) Dermatomyositis (DM)- classical skin findings with muscle weakness. A subgroup of patients has skin findings with no clinical muscle disease and are characterized as clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis (CADM). Antisynthetase syndrome (ASyS)- presence of anti-aminoacyl transfer RNA (tRNA) synthetase antibodies (ASAs) with interstitial lung disease (ILD), inflammatory myopathy, arthritis, and/or mechanic’s hands. Overlap myositis (OM)- inflammatory myopathy with simultaneous presence of features of other autoimmune diseases such as systemic sclerosis (SSc), mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), or Sjögren’s syndrome. Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) - myopathy with muscle biopsy features of myonecrosis without significant inflammatory cells. Inclusion body myositis (IBM) - asymmetric myopathy at disease onset presenting with distal muscle weakness. Muscle biopsy demonstrates endomysial inflammatory infiltrate and muscle fibers with rimmed vacuoles and eosinophilic muscle fiber inclusions. Polymyositis - myositis with the absence of features that would classify patients in the other subgroups. IIMs can affect multiple compartments of the respiratory system including lung parenchyma resulting in ILD, pulmonary vasculature leading to pulmonary hypertension (PH), and respiratory muscles. Aspiration pneumonitis/pneumonia from dysphagia is also seen. ILD is the most common pulmonary manifestation, with an overall estimated prevalence of 40 - 50%. However, in patients with CADM and ASyS the prevalence is over 80%. ILD in IIM can be progressive and carries high morbidity and mortality. This review will discuss pulmonary and extrapulmonary clinical manifestations of IIM-ILD, diagnostic work-up, treatment options, management approach and future directions. We focus on ASyS and DM, which most commonly involve the lungs, however the principles can apply to any phenotype of IIM lung disease. Pathobiology The underlying mechanism of IIM is postulated to be chronic inflammation caused by both innate and adaptive immune activation triggered by interactions between genetic and environmental risk factors ( ). Several HLA and non-HLA genetic associations have been demonstrated in IIM. , Epidemiologic studies have reported numerous environmental risk factors including smoking. Preceding respiratory and gastrointestinal infections - including COVID19 infection have been associated with IIM onset. - Medications such as statins, immune check point inhibitors, d-penicillamine, interferons, and anti-tumor necrosis factor agents are also potential triggers. - A seasonal distribution associated with increased ultraviolet radiation exposure is reported in anti-Jo-1 antibody IIM. , ASyS is characterized by the development of autoantibodies directed against different tRNA-synthetase enzymes. In genetically susceptible individuals, activation of adaptive immune cells and tolerance breakdown leads to antigen presentation, CD8-T cell priming, and CD4-T cell-B cell crosstalk. Release of type I/II interferons, B lymphocyte stimulator, and other cytokines lead to the production of anti-tRNA synthetase autoantibodies. - The resultant aberrant immune activation of T cells, including CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, is thought to play a central role in disease pathogenesis. Activated CD8+ T cells release granzyme B, which cleaves several aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases in the lungs. Active T/B cells and autoantibodies enter the systemic circulation and encounter the altered autoantigens in the lungs, resulting in lung injury. Of the twenty known aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, antibodies against ten have been identified. The most common is anti-histidyl-tRNA-synthetase antibody or anti-Jo-1 antibody. MDA5 is an intracellular protein that helps recognize viral RNA as danger signals. Viral infections might incite autoimmunity through several possible mechanisms. Viral induced MDA5 activation followed by excessive cellular apoptosis could lead to a tolerance breach and development of disease. , Clinical presentation and diagnostic testing The classical presentation of IIM includes a combination of muscle, skin, lung, and joint disease. However, patients may initially manifest symptoms affecting any of these systems in isolation. The disease can become progressive and affect other organs after initial presentation. A multidisciplinary collaboration between pulmonology, rheumatology, dermatology, and neurology plays an important role in the diagnosis and management of these patients, particularly when they do not present with muscle weakness. MAA include antibodies such as anti-PM/Scl, anti-U1RNP, anti-U3RNP, anti-Ku, and anti-Ro52. Several single and multiplex commercial assays are available for detecting the majority of MSAs. These assays include enzyme-linked Immunosorbent assays, addressable laser bead Immunoassays, immunoblotting techniques, and RNA or protein radio-immunoprecipitation. Currently, the gold standard for myositis autoantibody testing is the radio-immunoprecipitation assay. Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) testing is often used to “screen” for CTD. However, it is not useful for detecting the presence of an MSA. Indirect Immunofluorescence using human epithelial type 2 cells as a substrate is the standard screening for ANA with quantification of the titer and ANA staining pattern. Most MSAs will yield a negative ANA result and thus a negative ANA does not rule out ASyS. We suggest starting with a panel that includes all eight available ASAs, anti-MDA-5, and anti-Ro52, which are antibodies that have been associated with ILD. Other antibodies such as anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP, or anti-CN1A can be ordered if clinically indicated. MSA-negative IIM-ILD Patients may present with clinical features consistent with IIM-ILD without myositis-specific autoantibodies. Within this group, those with ILD as the first clinical manifestation represent a more challenging subgroup that requires evaluation by a multidisciplinary team of experts in IIM-ILD. Currently, standard assays only identify the eight most common ASAs that have been associated with IIM-ILD. However, there are other tRNA synthetases whose corresponding autoantibodies are not yet identified by standard assays. Immunoprecipitation is particularly useful in this population of MSA-negative IIM-ILD patients, as it may reveal an immunoprecipitation band representing an unidentified autoantibody. In our practice, we have observed that a significant number of MSA-negative patients have a positive anti-Ro-52 autoantibody. Sclafani et al. reported that 50 ILD patients with only a positive anti-Ro-52 autoantibody had similar outcomes compared to those with co-positivity of anti-Ro-52 and an MSA. This highlights the potential role of the anti-Ro-52 autoantibody in the evaluation of patients with suspected IIM-ILD, particularly those with negative MSA. These patients exhibit a higher mean percent-predicted FVC and lower total HRCT scores compared to patients with the anti-Jo1 autoantibody. Yoshifuji et al. reported that MSA-negative patients had similar lung function, lower ILD recurrence, and a lower response to steroids compared to those who tested positive for Larger studies and the use of novel immunoassays that can detect other ASA will help to better characterize this group. Pulmonary Manifestations Interstitial lung disease - ILD is the most common pulmonary manifestation of IIM, affecting over 80% of patients with ASyS and anti-MDA5. - . In other IIM subtypes, ILD is less prevalent, milder, and often presents with muscle disease. Lung disease preceding extra pulmonary symptoms is seen in 16-65 % of patients, often by several months. Three distinct clinical presentations of IIM-ILD are frequently encountered: Rapidly progressive ILD (RP-ILD) can be seen in an acute exacerbation of previously undiagnosed ILD or in patients with significant worsening of ILD within three months of diagnosis. Acute hypoxic respiratory failure is commonly associated with anti-MDA5 DM and ASyS, particularly anti-Jo1, anti-PL7 and anti-PL12 antibodies. Development of spontaneous pneumomediastinum is a sign of poor prognosis. Chronic ILD (C-ILD) manifests as insidious onset of dyspnea and cough, which can be associated with extra-pulmonary symptoms of IIM. It is the most common presentation in ASyS patients. Sub-clinical ILD can be seen on imaging with minimal or no symptoms, particularly in patients with anti-SAE, anti-SRP and anti-TIF1γ antibodies, which are associated with severe myositis . Occasionally, ASyS patients might be in this category when extrapulmonary symptoms are predominant . Chest imaging is important in establishing diagnosis, choosing therapy, and estimating prognosis of IIM-ILD ( ). A high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan (< 1.5 mm slices) with volumetric scanning of the chest with inspiratory, and expiratory images can help characterize parenchymal disease. Prone images can assist with subtle, sub-pleural changes and distinguish from compression atelectasis or dependent edema. Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) is the most common pattern in C-ILD and is seen in over 50 % of patients with IIM-ILD. It is characterized by peripheral and lower lobe predominant reticulation and ground glass opacities with sub-pleural sparing . Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) is the most common pattern in C-ILD and is seen in over 50 % of patients with IIM-ILD. It is characterized by peripheral and lower lobe predominant reticulation and ground glass opacities with sub-pleural sparing . Organizing pneumonia (OP) pattern is characterized by patchy peripheral or peribronchovascular consolidation and ground glass opacities. The presence of an OP pattern on imaging is associated with a good response to immunosuppression and better outcomes. Concomitant presence of both NSIP and OP patterns are often observed in IIM-ILD. A usual intestinal pneumonia (UIP) pattern is characterized by sub-pleural, predominantly basilar fibrosis, honeycombing, and absence of ground glass opacities. UIP has been reported in 10 to 30% of patients with ASyS, usually in advanced disease . Additional radiographic features have been associated with UIP due to CTD. They include the concentration of fibrosis in the anterior upper lobes, exuberant honeycomb like cysts in the fibrotic parenchyma, lower lobe predominant fibrosis with sharp demarcation with normal lung in the craniocaudal plane. The diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) pattern consists of diffuse ground glass opacities and consolidation. It is commonly seen during an acute exacerbation of C-ILD or in RP-ILD, particularly in patients with anti-MDA5 DM and ASyS. UIP and DAD patterns are associated with poor response to treatment and worse outcomes. The imaging patterns can overlap, evolve, and progress. , Pulmonary function test (PFT) - A restrictive pattern (low total lung capacity and low forced vital capacity [FVC]) on PFT along with a low diffusion of carbon monoxide (DLCO) is the most common finding on PFTs. Patients with mild disease may have an isolated mild reduction in DLCO with normal FVC. Concomitant ILD and emphysema or PH may lead to a reduction in DLCO which is out of proportion to the reduction in FVC reduction. In patients with respiratory muscle weakness, PFTs usually reveal a decreased FVC, normal DLCO, a greater than 20% drop in FVC when laying supine and decreased maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures. Pathology (<xref rid="SD1" ref-type="supplementary-material">Figure S1</xref>)- Lung biopsy is rarely needed to establish a diagnosis of IIM-ILD with classical clinical, radiographic, and serological presentations. Occasionally, it may be needed to rule out malignancy. NSIP is the most common pathological finding. A UIP pattern is seen in a minority of patients. Both NSIP and UIP may be associated with an acute pathology, either DAD or OP. Pulmonary hypertension (PH) has been reported in 8 to 10% of patients with ASyS and is associated with decreased survival . Echocardiogram is used as a screening test to determine if further work-up for PH is warranted, but the clinician needs to maintain a high clinical suspicion as echocardiography in patients with parenchymal lung disease may be inaccurate. The diagnosis of PH requires confirmation by right heart catheterization. In patients with concomitant advanced ILD, PH is classified as World Symposium for Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) group 3 disease. However, pulmonary arterial hypertension (WSPH group 1) can also occur in IIM . Rarely, PH can be a consequence of myocarditis, inflammatory infiltration in the cardiac conduction system and replacement fibrosis (WSPH group 2). Patients may present with angina, dysrhythmias, or congestive heart failure. Cardiac MRI is a sensitive technique that can detect mild inflammation in the myocardium. , Respiratory muscle disease- Respiratory muscle (diaphragm, intercostal muscles) weakness can present with dyspnea and orthopnea and can progress to hypercapnic respiratory failure if severe. Isolated respiratory muscle involvement is rare. However, subclinical diaphragm weakness is common and can be seen in up to 75% of patients, often with mild symptoms or normal PFT. Dyspnea in the absence of parenchymal or pulmonary vascular disease should trigger work-up for muscle weakness. Diaphragmatic ultrasound is a promising, non-invasive method to assess diaphragm function by measuring diaphragm dome excursion and diaphragm thickness. It can accurately measure diaphragm function in other neuromuscular diseases, but clinical utility in IIM is yet to be established. Aspiration- Dysphagia can occur due to pharyngeal muscle weakness or esophageal dysmotility. In the EuroMyositis registry, 26% of patients with ASyS and 53% of those with OM reported dysphagia . This can lead to aspiration pneumonia or pneumonitis. Video-fluoroscopic swallowing study and manometry can be used to evaluate dysphagia. Musculoskeletal manifestations: (<xref rid="SD1" ref-type="supplementary-material">Figure S2</xref>) Myopathy is a hallmark feature of IIM. The characteristic presentation is symmetric, proximal muscle weakness with hip and thigh muscles being the most frequently affected areas. Common symptoms are difficulty standing from a seated position, climbing steps, or raising arms overhead. Neck extensor muscle weakness can cause head drop and pharyngeal muscle weakness may result in dysphagia and voice change. Myalgia and muscle tenderness are common with ASyS. A detailed neurologic examination is critical in determining the severity and distribution of muscle weakness and to rule out myositis mimics. In patients with ASyS, lung disease in the absence of or preceding myositis by months is typical . Absence of myopathy is most often seen in anti-MDA5 DM but can also be associated with other MSAs. CADM patients are at higher risk of developing ILD compared to classic DM patients, and CADM is considered a predictor of RP-ILD. - Diagnostic work up for myopathy includes a variable combination of muscle enzymes, muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), electromyography, and muscle biopsy. Creatine kinase (CK) is the most sensitive measurable muscle enzyme and can be used to monitor treatment responses and relapses. Other non-specific biomarkers of muscle injury include aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase and aminotransferases. Bilateral thigh MRI using a myositis protocol (T1-weighted imaging, fluid-sensitive T2W with fat suppression or short-tau inversion recovery sequence) can be used to identify early stages of myositis and target areas for a muscle biopsy. Findings include edema of muscle fibers, alteration in muscle signal intensity and in later stages presence of fatty infiltration, fibrosis, or muscle atrophy. These changes are not specific to myositis and can also be seen in injuries, muscle infarction, denervation, or rhabdomyolysis. - Electromyography can distinguish myopathy from neuropathic causes of weakness. Myopathy is characterized by polyphasic motor unit action potentials that are of short-duration, low amplitude on voluntary activation and prominent muscle membrane irritability at rest. Electromyography is not diagnostic of myositis, as similar findings can occur in infectious, toxic, metabolic or degenerative myopathies. It can guide muscle biopsy, but muscle biopsy should not be performed on a muscle that has recently undergone electromyography testing. - Arthritis or arthralgia is seen in 90% of IIM patients and is the presenting symptom in 30% of ASyS patients. Three general patterns of joint involvement are seen: i)- symmetrical, non-erosive, polyarthritis affecting the hand joints and knees (~60%), ii) isolated joint arthralgia (25%), and iii) subluxing arthropathy affecting the distal interphalangeal joints (15%). Plain radiographs typically demonstrate non-destructive arthropathy, although erosive arthritis has been reported in a minority of cases. Skin manifestations: (<xref rid="F3" ref-type="fig">Figure 3</xref>) The presence of classical skin findings, on history or examination, can be helpful in establishing a diagnosis; however, the appearance of skin manifestations can be impacted by the individual patient’s skin tone. Several pathognomonic DM skin findings have been described and can be seen in various combinations in IIM: Heliotrope rash (periorbital violaceous erythema commonly with edema) Gottron papules (erythematous-to-violaceous papules and plaques, overlying metacarpo-phalangeal and interphalangeal joints) Gottron sign (erythematous macules or patches over extensor surfaces of joints) Shawl sign (erythema over posterior shoulders, neck, and upper back) V sign (erythema over lower anterior neck and upper chest) Nailfold changes (Periungual nailfold erythema, telangiectasia, punctate cuticular hemorrhage) Holster sign (symmetric poikiloderma of hips and lateral thighs) Mechanic’s hands- non-pruritic, hyperkeratotic eruptions on the lateral surface of fingers. Common in ASyS patients. Most of the skin lesions are pruritic or burning and some can be photosensitive. Skin hypo/hyperpigmentation, atrophy, and telangiectasia resulting in poikiloderma can occur, especially on the upper chest and lateral upper arms. Patients with anti-MDA5 DM may develop relatively specific skin features, including skin erosions, ulcerations over joints or on digits, and tender palmar papules. Furthermore, cancer is a leading cause of death in adults with IIM. , Various cancers including lung, ovarian, colorectal, breast, lymphoma and nasopharyngeal cancer are amongst the most common forms. The risk and screening strategies vary significantly based on the disease phenotype and antibody profile. Patients with DM (anti-TIF1γ, NXP-2 ab) with age >40 years at IIM onset, dysphagia and cutaneous necrosis are at the highest risk for having an underlying malignancy followed by patients with PM, IMNM or CADM, who are at intermediate risk. Patients with ASA (Anti-Jo1, Non-Jo1 Ab), MAA or Anti-SRP antibody with features of Raynaud phenomenon, inflammatory arthropathy and ILD are low risk. Based on risk stratification, screening for occult malignancies with imaging, cancer markers, whole body positron emission tomography scans should be considered. Classification criteria of IIM (<xref rid="T2" ref-type="table">Table 2</xref>) Bohan and Peter provided classification criteria for DM in 1975, which was widely used for 40 years. , They included characteristic DM rashes and the need to exclude other causes of myopathy but did not mention pulmonary manifestations. Patients with anti-Jo-1 Ab were recognized as having a distinct phenotype termed ASyS in the early 90s. , Since then, IIMs have been further classified based on clinical manifestations and antibody profiles. In 2017, the first validated classification criteria of IIM by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) were developed and provided the probability of having IIM. The criteria include age of onset, pattern of muscle weakness, muscle enzyme elevation, muscle biopsy findings, presence of rash, and anti-Jo-1 Ab. It did not include ILD, or non-Jo-1 antibodies. The criteria also do not define ASyS as a distinct IIM subtype. There are active efforts for establishing a revised classification criteria for IIM and separate classification criteria for ASyS. Currently, criteria suggested by Solomon et al and Connor et al based-on expert opinion, are widely used to establish a diagnosis of ASyS. Presence of anti-synthetase antibodies with any one or two clinical features (ILD, IIM, RP, skin changes) can be considered adequate for diagnosing ASyS , . Management Immunosuppression is the mainstay of treatment of IIM-ILD targeting several pathways. As with most rare diseases, few clinical trials exist, and treatment varies based on clinical presentation and center preference. The American College of Rheumatology is finalizing guidelines for management of CTD-ILD, which appear consistent with our approach outlined here . Patients with RP-ILD need early, aggressive, combination anti-inflammatory therapy. Patients with C-ILD can be treated in “step-up” escalation of therapy over months. Patients with subclinical disease can be monitored without therapy but require close follow-up. Treatment decisions are based on expert opinion, experience, the “clinical gestalt” of individual treatment teams and require multi-disciplinary collaboration. Table 3 summarizes our recommendations on starting dosing, common adverse events, and monitoring of several immunosuppressant agents used in patients with IIM-ILD. Corticosteroids Corticosteroids (CS) have been the first-line treatment for pulmonary and extra-pulmonary manifestations of IIM for decades. A meta-analysis of patients with IIM-ILD (45% ASyS, 40 % DM), reviewed the impact of various treatment strategies. Six studies in the analysis included 124 patients who received CS monotherapy. A significant improvement was reported in 89% of the patients. However, the meta-analysis had several limitations and none of the included studies were controlled. Most studies evaluating other therapies for IIM-ILD have patients on background CS, thus limiting data on using a “steroid-free” approach. In clinical practice, most patients are started on CS at time of diagnosis either as a single agent or in combination with a steroid-sparing agent. Advantages of CS include quick onset, low cost, and physician experience. However, long-term use of CS carries significant morbidity. Given the significant morbidity associated with long-term CS, we advocate to start them in conjunction with a steroid-sparing agent early in the course of disease. Anti-metabolites Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), methotrexate, and azathioprine inhibit lymphocyte activation and proliferation by inhibiting DNA synthesis through various mechanisms. In patients with IIM-ILD, they are commonly used as first-line steroid sparing agent due to good patient tolerance and favorable adverse effect profiles. However, data are limited to retrospective studies. In a single-center retrospective study of 125 CTD-ILD patients (32 with IIM), MMF led to improvement or stabilization of disease across various underlying CTDs. Patients with UIP pathology demonstrated stabilization and those with non-UIP had improvement in lung function. In a retrospective review of patients with IIM-ILD, both MMF and azathioprine led to improvement or stabilization of lung function (FVC improvement 3.6% in MMF group, 3.3% in azathioprine group) and a significant reduction in prednisone dose (6.9 mg in MMF group, 15 mg in azathioprine group) at 24 months. The rate of medication adverse effects was slightly higher in the azathioprine group . Mira-Avendano et al. compared cyclophosphamide, azathioprine and MMF as second-line agents in steroid-refractory IIM-ILD and reported that all three led to an improvement in FVC, DLCO and dyspnea scores at 12 months. We recommend testing for thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) deficiency in patients taking azathioprine as TPMT intermediate metabolizers require lower doses, and poor metabolizers should not receive azathioprine. Methotrexate has been efficacious in treating myositis and has a steroid-sparing effect; however, data in ILD is scarce. Casal-Dominguez compared methotrexate and azathioprine monotherapy in 102 ASyS patients. Both drugs led to improvement in muscle strength, reduced CS dose requirement, and a similar rate of adverse effects. However, 4% of patients developed methotrexate pneumonitis. While the use of methotrexate remains a viable alternative to other anti-metabolites drugs, clinicians must be aware of the risk of pneumonitis. Calcineurin Inhibitors (CNI) The CNIs, tacrolimus and cyclosporine, inhibit T cell function by inhibiting the enzyme calcineurin and impairing transcription of cytokines such as interlukin-2. In a randomized controlled trial (RCT) in patients with IIM- ILD, Fujisawa et al. compared the use of tacrolimus and cyclosporine as first add-on agents in 58 patients with IIM-ILD (47% CADM, 33% DM, 20% PM. Patients in both groups showed similar improvement in FVC (19% tacrolimus, 16% cyclosporine) and DLCO (14% tacrolimus, 9% cyclosporine). This trial demonstrated efficacy of CNI as first-line agents with CS but was not designed to compare them to other treatments . Therefore, CNIs can be used as first- or second-line steroid-sparing agents. The choice between tacrolimus and cyclosporine is physician-dependent, with no evidence of superiority for either agent. Rituximab Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody which leads to peripheral B cell depletion. The RECITAL RCT compared rituximab and cyclophosphamide as second-line agents in 101 CTD-ILD patients (44 with IIM-ILD). Both rituximab and cyclophosphamide increased the median FVC at 24 weeks (94 ml rituximab, 99 ml cyclophosphamide) and 48 weeks (112 ml rituximab, 138 ml cyclophosphamide). DLCO, six min walk distance (6MWD), and quality of life also improved in both groups. The cyclophosphamide group had more total adverse effects but similar serious adverse events. This RCT demonstrated that most patients treated with second line rituximab or cyclophosphamide improve, with similar efficacy of both agents. Retrospective studies have shown similar efficacy of cyclophosphamide and rituximab and a better adverse effect profile with rituximab. In a systematic review of patients with anti-MDA5 ILD, 71% of patients responded to rituximab as a second- or third-line agent. Rituximab can be used as a second-line agent in refractory disease. Cyclophosphamide Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent, commonly used for cancer chemotherapy. It is used for induction in life-threatening autoimmune conditions due to its rapid and profound immune suppression. In addition to data from the RECITAL RCT (see above), similar findings were seen in a systematic review of five studies analyzing cyclophosphamide use in IIM- ILD patients (55 % anti-Jo-1 Ab). In this review, 71% of patients had improvement in FVC, 69% had improvement in DLCO, and 67% had improvement in chest CT findings. Cyclophosphamide can be administered up to six months in severe or RP-ILD, with transition to less toxic agents once disease is in remission. Fan et al. compared tofacitinib with tacrolimus in a retrospective study of patients with anti-MDA5 DM. Over 50% of patients had RP-ILD. Lower mortality in tofacitinib group was seen at six months (38.5% vs 62.9%) and one year (44.0% vs 65.7%). It has also shown efficacy in patients with disease refractory to other agents. Tofacitinib is orally dosed and can be used as a second- or third-line agent in anti-MDA5 DM. Intravenous immune globulin (IVIg) IVIg is purified from pooled human plasma, consisting of monomeric Immunoglobulin G. IVIg has shown efficacy in treating DM patients, with decreased disease activity compared to placebo. In IIM-ILD, data are limited. In a retrospective study, 17 ASyS patients (80% with refractory disease) were treated with IVIg for six months and followed for two years; FVC % and DLCO % increased, and prednisone dose decreased . Most patients were on concomitant immune suppression. The lack of a control group limits the ability to conclude efficacy. The main indication for IVIg in IIM is to treat extra-pulmonary disease and as second- or third-line therapy in RP- ILD. The side effect profile of IVIg and lack of immunosuppression makes it an attractive add on therapy in patients with severe lung disease or in patients where active infections have not been ruled out. Anti-fibrotic therapy Nintedanib and pirfenidone have demonstrated efficacy in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The INBUILD RCT studied the efficacy of nintedanib in 663 patients with progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF). In this study, 25 % of the included patients had CTD-ILD. Nintedanib slowed the rate of progression in the entire cohort. Data from patients with IIM-ILD were not reported separately . In a single center, prospective study of patients with IIM-ILD, 39 patients on nintedanib were compared to those receiving standard-of-care therapy. Patients in the nintedanib group had a lower RP-ILD risk and better survival compared to controls. In the 2022 American Thoracic Society guidelines for PPF, nintedanib is recommended for PPF patients. Pirfenidone did not meet its primary endpoint in patients with PPF in the RELIEF trial. However, the study had to be stopped due to poor recruitment and futility. The determination of disease progression can be challenging in ILD, particularly in IIM-ILD. Clinicians should give a trial of adequate immunosuppressive treatment with step-up as indicated after the initial diagnosis before using antifibrotics. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) TPE can decrease the levels of autoantibodies, cytokines, and immune complexes. Data on TPE in IIM-ILD is limited to case series. In a retrospective study of 11 patients who underwent TPE for anti-MDA 5 ILD, survival was 90% in the TPE group compared to 50 % in the non-TPE group. With limited data, TPE continues to be used as a salvage therapy for RP-ILD. Lung transplantation Lung transplantation is an option for selected patients with end-stage lung disease. Patients with progressive disease despite appropriate therapy, need for supplemental oxygen, progressive fibrotic disease, and RP- ILD should be considered for transplant evaluation. In addition to standard issues of candidate selection, extra-pulmonary manifestations of IIM can impact candidacy and post-transplant outcomes. Active myositis can affect rehabilitation potential, ventilator weaning and risk of aspiration. Therefore, it needs to be quiescent before transplant referral. Post-transplant outcomes in IIM-ILD are comparable to those for other indications in US and European cohorts. Timely referral to an experienced transplant center can help improve the likelihood of a successful transplant. Pulmonary rehabilitation Pulmonary rehabilitation is a comprehensive intervention for patients with chronic lung disease that includes exercise training and education, usually in an outpatient setting. A Cochrane review of 16 trials in patients with ILD demonstrated that pulmonary rehabilitation helped to improve 6MWD, dyspnea, and quality of life, with no significant adverse effects. This treatment modality remains underutilized despite high reward and low risk profile. Referral should be considered in all symptomatic patients with IIM-ILD. Infection prevention and prophylaxis Patients on immune suppression are at increased risk for infectious complications. Prophylaxis for pneumocystis pneumonia with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or an alternate regimen is started in patients on two immune-suppression medications or those on high dose corticosteroids (greater than 20 mg/ day prednisone for one month). Age and location specific immunization prior initiation of immune suppression as well as seasonal annual immunization is strongly recommended. Management of PH In patients with WSPH group I PAH, treatment according to the latest WSPH guidelines for group 1 disease should be pursued. Immune suppression has been reported to be beneficial in observational studies in patients with systematic lupus erythematosus and MCTD associated PH. However there is no supporting data in patients with IIM related PH. In patients with WSPH Group 3 PH due to ILD, inhaled treprostinil is recommended as it has shown to increase 6MWD (mean increase 31m), improve biomarkers of right heart failure (nt-pro BNP) and decrease the incidence of clinical deterioration (22 % vs 33%). Management of respiratory muscle weakness Aggressive immune modulation with high-dose steroids, IVIg and other agents should be initiated depending on the degree of muscle weakness. Patients need to be monitored closely for worsening disease with measurements of negative inspiratory force and vital capacity. A negative inspiratory force of less than 30 cmH2O and FVC of less than 20ml/kg may warrant monitoring in an intensive care unit setting. Patients may progress to respiratory failure and require noninvasive or invasive mechanical ventilation. Management in this situation is similar to other neuromuscular diseases affecting the respiratory system. Noninvasive ventilation can help improve hypercapnia, sleep quality and quality of life in patients with chronic hypoventilation. Treatment approach (<xref rid="F4" ref-type="fig">Figure 4</xref>) Our management approach is based on disease acuity, severity, and co-morbidities. Specific antibody profiles can help predict clinical course, but we do not use them in isolation to make treatment decisions. In patients with incidental, mild, or subclinical disease with no symptoms and normal pulmonary physiology, a “wait and watch” approach can be adopted. We closely monitor for the development of symptoms and measure PFT every 3 to 6 months to look for any signs of progression. In C-ILD patients, we use a “step- up” approach starting with a single agent, monitoring response, and stepping up treatment over weeks or months. First line therapy includes moderate dose CS (prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg), with tapering over 2-3 months to the lowest tolerated dose. Depending on severity, we often start an antimetabolite within weeks. We use rituximab or CNIs as second-line agents either alone or in combination with IVIG. Cyclophosphamide can be used as a third-line agent in refractory disease. Anti-fibrotic medications are added in PPF if there is progression on optimal anti-inflammatory therapies. In patients with RP-ILD we start with early “aggressive” therapy to induce remission, followed by a “step down” approach once the disease is quiescent. The favored regimen varies based on experience and institution but includes a combination of high dose CS and one or two immunomodulators (CNI, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, IVIg and tofacitinib). Lung transplantation should be considered early in patients with single-organ disease and respiratory failure. Several retrospective studies have reported the utility of combination Immune suppression in patients with anti-MDA5 ILD . Prognosis Estimated one-year survival in patients with IIM-ILD is over 90%- and ten-year cumulative survival is ~80% .When compared to patients with IPF, survival is significantly better in IIM-ILD. Patients with anti-MDA5 DM continue to have a high short-term mortality, with 75% one-year survival , , .Acute exacerbations of ILD carry a high short-term mortality irrespective of underlying IIM. The overall age-adjusted mortality rate for IIM-ILD in the US has been stable for the past two decades .Factors associated with lower survival are anti- MDA5 positivity, older age at onset, RP-ILD, poor response to therapy, elevated inflammatory markers, UIP pattern, malignancy, and concomitant PH , . Conclusion and Future directions IIMs are a common cause of chronic and RP-ILD, often with isolated lung disease. Recognition of IIM as a cause of ILD is essential since most patients respond to initial immunosuppressive treatment. The widespread availability of MAA/MSA testing can help improve diagnosis and phenotyping of this disease. Notably, there is lack of reliable biomarkers to guide therapy and monitor the clinical response.

Conclusion and Future directions IIMs are a common cause of chronic and RP-ILD, often with isolated lung disease. Recognition of IIM as a cause of ILD is essential since most patients respond to initial immunosuppressive treatment. The widespread availability of MAA/MSA testing can help improve diagnosis and phenotyping of this disease. Notably, there is lack of reliable biomarkers to guide therapy and monitor the clinical response. Further, better diagnostic criteria for IIM should recognize isolated IIM-ILD (“pneumo-myositis”) and ASyS. The guidelines may help standardize diagnosis and aid in treatment trials. Several treatments continue to be investigated in patients with IIM, with many ongoing clinical trials. Immune modulators targeting various pathways are being repurposed for use in IIM-ILD. Case reports have shown benefit with daratumumab (anti CD38 ab), basiliximab (IL-2 receptor antagonist), tocilizumab (IL-6 antagonist), abatacept (selective costimulation modulator), anakinra (interleukin-1 receptor antagonist) and ruxolitinib (JAK inhibitor) amongst others , .The infusion of chimeric antigen receptor T cells that recognize CD19 + B cells can lead to their depletion and an “immune reset”. This therapy has shown promise in inducing remission in patients with refractory SLE . Two recent case reports demonstrated remission in patients with refractory ASyS with chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy , .While this is encouraging, data is scant, and this is still considered investigational. chunks.content: Introduction Heart transplantation (HTx) continues to be the definitive treatment for patients with end-stage heart disease of varying etiologies, with more than 6,000 heart transplants performed annually worldwide [ ]. Nevertheless, the long-term survival and quality of prognosis are constrained by post-HTx complications, including cardiac allograft rejection (CAR), cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) and primary graft dysfunction (PGD) [ , ]. Current surveillance of CAR relies heavily on invasive endomyocardial biopsies (EMBx), which are associated with a complication rate of 2.3%, age restrictions, and potential sampling errors [ – ]. Invasive coronary angiography (ICA) and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) are diagnostic procedures for CAV, with significant costs and potential complications, such as bleeding, infection, and acute kidney injury, which are not suitable for all recipients [ , ]. PGD, an early idiopathic ventricular dysfunction after HTx. The RADIAL score is the only effective scoring system that can predict the clinical risk of PGD, an early idiopathic ventricular dysfunction after HTx; however, it lacks accuracy [ ]. Omics technologies are becoming increasingly accessible and can be used to identify novel biomarkers while revealing the underlying biology of various diseases. These technologies have emerged as transformative tools for identifying potential circulating biomarkers for rejection monitoring and post-transplant injuries [ – ]. Leveraging multi-omics methodologies, which encompass genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics analyses, has significantly advanced our understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms governing allograft complications in HTx [ – ]. Single-cell and multi-omics analyses have gained considerable attention in the pursuit of clinical transformations because of their ability to dissect cellular heterogeneity and capture dynamic molecular changes that may serve as potential therapeutic targets [ , ]. Machine learning, with its capacity to process extensive datasets and identify intricate patterns, has demonstrated promise for the development of predictive models for adverse events following transplantation [ ]. Despite standard combinations of immunosuppressants administered to HTx recipients, research and innovations in immunosuppressive therapy over the past two decades remain lacking. This stagnation is partly attributed to a poor understanding of biomarkers associated with immunosuppression. Identifying actionable risk biomarkers for post-transplant adverse events could facilitate the personalization of conventional one-size-fits-all post-transplant management paradigms. These approaches enhance the survival rates and reduce the incidence of adverse events in HTx recipients. With the application of these technologies in clinical settings, a deeper understanding of individualized factors that affect prognosis, such as recipient age, sex, and race, should be considered [ , , ]. This state-of-the-art review aims to systematically summarize the applications of multi-omics technologies in HTx, and to describe the value and future directions of these technologies in the clinical transformation of heart transplant care. Omics applications in CAR and early graft injury Prediction of CAR and early graft injury Genomics analysis has identified thousands of DNA sequences that are widely used in HTx (Table ). Donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA) serves as a non-invasive biomarker for CAR and includes both acute cellular rejection (ACR) and antibody-mediated rejection (AMR). This approach is recommended by the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) and the American Society of Transplantation (AST) [ – ]. The Genomic Research Alliance for Transplantation (GRAfT) conducted a multi-center prospective study involving 165 transplant recipients, where genetic profiling was used to determine donor-recipient single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Unbiased shotgun sequencing was employed to quantify the proportion of plasma dd-cfDNA relative to total cfDNA (%dd-cfDNA). The study confirmed that an elevated percentage of dd-cfDNA was correlated with both the severity of CAR and early graft injury (p < 0.001).When the %dd-cfDNA threshold was set at ≥ 0.25, the area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve ranged from 89 to 95%, demonstrating excellent sensitivity and specificity, with a negative predictive value (NPV) reaching 99%. Furthermore, 81% of myocardial EMBx can be avoided when % dd-cfDNA level remains < 0.25 [ ]. Informative SNPs refer to instances in which the recipient has a homozygous genotype (two alleles with the same nucleotide) that differs from the donor’s genotype, which may be either a heterozygous or homozygous variant. These SNPs can be used to distinguish between donor and recipient DNA [ , , ]. Whole-genome sequencing, based on informative SNPs, allows for the precise quantification of dd-cfDNA and provides strong evidence that an elevated %dd-cfDNA is associated with CAR [ ]. However, pre-transplant DNA genotyping to identify SNPs increases the complexity of non-invasive screening. To address this, multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) targeting SNPs can be used without prior genotyping of the donor or recipient, enabling the quantification of dd-cfDNA through next-generation sequencing (NGS) based on informative SNPs [ , ].
